lit.title: How does a device-problem code get onto a MAUDE report, and what does that make it as an answer key?

report.answer: The device-problem code on a MAUDE report is the code the person filing the report typed in. Nobody independent assigns it, and nobody checks it afterwards. Manufacturers enter it in field H6 of Form 3500A, sent electronically (eMDR). Importers and user facilities use field F10. Manufacturer reports make up roughly 95% of MAUDE: Ensign and Cohen (2017) put user-facility, voluntary and distributor reports together at about 5%. FDA's instructions ask filers to pick the code that "most accurately describe[s]" the problem, at the lowest and most specific level, as many codes as needed, and never a parent together with its own child. FDA says it reviews every report. I found no FDA document saying it re-codes reports, and Ensign and Cohen state the problem-code field is not checked when entered. A follow-up report (due within 30 days of new information, 21 CFR 803.56) can change the record, and MAUDE shows only the latest version. The code set itself moves every year. FDA switched to the IMDRF terms around 2020-21. In the 2025 update (19 Sep 2025) Annex A gained 3 terms, changed 16 and retired 3 (A0202-A0204). In the 2026 update (17 Aug 2026), which falls inside the project's test window, 43 Annex A terms were changed. One more mechanism produces template text with a habitual code: since 2018 manufacturers may file quarterly summary malfunction reports, one for each brand × model × problem-code combination, whose narrative must open with "This report summarizes XXX malfunction events". No regulator (FDA, GAO, HHS OIG) has published an audit of how accurately codes are chosen. The academic evidence is thin: one dissertation judged 26.47% of 102 sampled codes inaccurate; one 2025 study found coding differs strongly by type of filer; one 2026 BMJ study found 57% of summary reports name no device or use problem. Nobody has measured how well trained coders agree with each other on Annex A codes. On "does everyone use it": MAUDE itself is used very widely in device-safety research. Using its device-problem code as a machine-learning answer key is rare. The only such study I found (Muaz et al. 2026) did not trust the filed codes: it kept only the 1,728 of 2,899 records where an LLM agreed with the filed code at level 2. Bottom line: the code is what the filer chose to enter, not what broke as judged by a trained coder. It is not a "wrong label" either. It is a different target: the filer's own, legally required classification, shaped by habit, templates and code-set versions. Matching it means predicting the filing, not finding the truth.

sources.citation: FDA, About the Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) Database (web page)
sources.says: Four reporter types: manufacturer, importer, user facility, voluntary (MW report numbers). Submitters are asked to enter the device-problem and patient-problem codes that most accurately describe the failure. Passive system with under-reporting, inaccuracies and unverified causation; not for estimating rates. Because of database limits, follow-up reports show only the most recent information. FDA reviews all MDRs.

sources.citation: FDA, MDR Adverse Event Codes (web page; updated 13 Apr 2026, content current as of 21 Aug 2026)
sources.says: Use the lowest, most specific code. More than one code is allowed, but not a parent together with its child. FDA codes map one-to-one to IMDRF codes. Updated with the yearly IMDRF maintenance. FDA no longer adds codes at manufacturers' request. eMDR accepts FDA, NCIt or IMDRF codes.

sources.citation: FDA, How to Code an MDR Adverse Event Report (web page)
sources.says: Importers and user facilities code in F10, manufacturers in H6. At least one code of each type is required (A, G, E, F; plus B, C, D for manufacturers). Use the most detailed code. If a placeholder code was used during an investigation, file a follow-up MDR with a different code once it is done. Code 3189 is for FDA use only. Nothing about FDA reviewing or re-coding.

sources.citation: FDA, Coding Resources for Medical Device Reports (web page; current as of 20 Aug 2026)
sources.says: Update log of IMDRF maintenance cycles: 5 Mar 2021; 19 Aug 2022 (Annex A +9 added, 6 modified); 30 Aug 2023 (A +4, 4 modified, retired A071205); 12 Aug 2024 (A +6, 4 modified); 19 Sep 2025 (A +3, 16 modified, retired A0202, A0203, A0204); 17 Aug 2026 (A 43 modified).

sources.citation: Ensign LG, Cohen KB. A Primer to the Structure, Content and Linkage of the FDA's MAUDE Files. eGEMs 2017
sources.says: About 5% of reports come from user facilities, voluntary reporters and distributors combined, so the rest come from manufacturers. About 32% of reports in the files carry a device problem code, and about a quarter of coded reports carry uninformative codes. The code field is not checked on entry, and filers sometimes enter codes for a different product.

sources.citation: 21 CFR 803.50, 803.52, 803.56 (Cornell LII copy of the eCFR)
sources.says: Manufacturers must report within 30 days of information that reasonably suggests a death, serious injury, or a malfunction likely to cause one if it recurred. They must investigate each event and submit what is reasonably known. 803.52(f)(6) requires evaluation codes per the MedWatch code instructions. 803.56: supplemental reports within 30 days of receiving new information, containing only new, changed or corrected details. (803.52 and 803.56 were also opened at law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/803.52 and /803.56.)

sources.citation: FDA, MDR Data Files (web page)
sources.says: The device problem code file holds codes from form sections F10 and H6. Each reporting source gets its own master record. Report types are initial, follow-up, extra copy, other. For voluntary reports, sections E to H hold no data.

sources.citation: FDA, Medical Device Reporting (MDR): How to Report Medical Device Problems (web page)
sources.says: FDA receives over two million MDRs a year and reviews all of them, together with supplemental reports. Lists the system's limitations (under-reporting, inaccuracies, unverified causation).

sources.citation: FDA, Voluntary Malfunction Summary Reporting Program (web page)
sources.says: Since the 2018 pilot (notice of 17 Aug 2018, updated 29 Aug 2024), manufacturers of eligible product codes file quarterly summary reports, one for each unique combination of brand, model and problem code(s). These appear in MAUDE.

sources.citation: FDA, Federal Register notice 2018-17770, Voluntary Malfunction Summary Reporting Program for Manufacturers, 17 Aug 2018 (GovInfo copy)
sources.says: The B5 narrative must begin 'This report summarizes XXX malfunction events' and then describe the events. Problem codes go in H6, and FDA expects the most specific appropriate code. Grouping is by brand × model × problem code.

sources.citation: FDA CDRH archived page, problem code concepts (c. 2009), UNT web archive
sources.says: The old codes were cleaned up: rarely used, ambiguous or duplicate codes were inactivated, synonyms merged ('Blockage' to 'Occlusion'), combined terms split. At least one device and one patient problem code per report, with no maximum. Does not say who codes.

sources.citation: Mishali M, Sheffer N, Mishali O, Negev M. Understanding Variation Among Medical Device Reporting Sources: A Study of the MAUDE Database. Clinical Therapeutics 47(1):76-81, 2025. doi:10.1016/j.clinthera.2024.10.004
sources.says: MAUDE 2005-2022, with device problem codes grouped by hand into device, user, clinical and unknown. Manufacturers' codes: 36.3% device issues, 32% unknown, 19.3% clinical. User facilities: 54.3% device issues, 30.8% use. Distributors: 85.7% clinical. Variation between reporter types is significant (P<0.00001).

sources.citation: Khanal D. Analyses of medical device failures related to computing technology. PhD dissertation, Rutgers University, 2018. doi:10.7282/T3TX3JPK
sources.says: In a sample of 102 computing-related MAUDE events (2007-2016), 62.74% lacked problem codes and 26.47% had inaccurate codes. The abstract does not say how accuracy was judged.

sources.citation: Muaz M, Janjua ZH, Loughran R, St John Lynch N. A Framework for LLM-Guided and ISO 5338-Aligned Data Engineering in Medical Device Adverse Event Reporting. AIAI 2026 preprint, 26 Apr 2026
sources.says: Says manufacturers code the reports and that the coding varies with human judgement. Keeps only records where Gemini Flash 3 agrees with the filed code at IMDRF level 2: 2,899 down to 1,728 device-problem records (40% dropped). Attributes the dropped records to hedged manufacturer language and some coding errors. GPT-OSS-120B agrees on the kept set at 59.49% at level 1 and 23.04% at level 3.

sources.citation: BMJ press release on: Evaluation of the accuracy, completeness, and compliance of current summary reporting of adverse events to the FDA using MAUDE: cross sectional study. BMJ 2026;395. doi:10.1136/bmj-2026-100812
sources.says: 6,308 summary reports covering 159,503 events (Jul 2019 - Jun 2025): 57% named no device or use problem, 38% reported insufficient information, 11% were wrongly marked as non-summary, 55% missed the 30-day deadline. Seen only through the press release.

sources.citation: Meier L, Wang EY, Tomes M, Redberg RF. Miscategorization of Deaths in the US FDA Adverse Events Database. JAMA Intern Med 2020;180(1):43-44
sources.says: 17.5% of Sapien 3 deaths and 24.7% of MitraClip deaths were filed as injury or malfunction events. This concerns the filer-chosen event type, not the problem code.

sources.citation: Emergo by UL, Global medical device adverse event coding (industry article)
sources.says: A24 = adverse event without identified device or use problem, A25 = no apparent adverse event, A26 = insufficient information, A27 = appropriate term/code not available. These are too general for meaningful trending. Annex A generally reflects the problem as complained; Annex C reflects investigation findings. Pick the most precise term.

sources.citation: Knisely BM et al. An Analysis of FDA Adverse Event Reporting Data for Trends in Medical Device Use Error. Proc HFES Health Care 9(1), 2020. doi:10.1177/2327857920091024
sources.says: Use-error codes make up 28.1% of reports that carry device problem codes (2010-2018). Cited by S14 as evidence of coding variation, but the abstract does not measure coding accuracy.

sources.citation: Trade press on the 2020 FDA/IMDRF harmonization (fdanews.com and criterionedge.com search results)
sources.says: FDA code sets were renamed to IMDRF names and eMDR began accepting IMDRF codes. Retired codes stopped being accepted on 28 Nov (2020), with full effect around February 2021.

findings.claim: The filer chooses the device-problem code: manufacturers in H6, importers and user facilities in F10. FDA's instruction is to pick the code(s) that most accurately describe the problem, at the most specific level.
findings.support: S1 (code paragraph); S3 (who codes, specificity); S2; S7 (codes come from F10/H6)

findings.claim: MAUDE is overwhelmingly manufacturer-filed: about 95% of reports come from manufacturers, about 5% from user facilities, voluntary reporters and distributors combined.
findings.support: S5 Background and Data Availability (older data); consistent with S12 abstract ('most reports come from manufacturers')

findings.claim: FDA reviews every report, but no FDA document I found says FDA re-codes or corrects the device-problem code. Ensign and Cohen state the code field is not checked on entry.

Annex A records the problem as complained or observed, not the investigated root cause (Annex C).

findings.support: S4 update log; S19 for the 2020-21 transition (snippet only)

findings.claim: Coding differs strongly by type of filer (manufacturer, user facility, distributor).
findings.support: S12 abstract

findings.support: S15 (press release only)

findings.support: Searches of fda.gov, gao.gov and oig.hhs.gov (the OIG 2009 report would not open because of a certificate error)

gaps: Could not open imdrf.org (timeouts), so the official Annex A definitions of A24-A27, the IMDRF N43 coding guidance and the Release 2025/2026 per-term change lists were not read. The project should diff its 2025 and 2026 code lists against the FDA XLSX (fda.gov/media/192166/download), which I did not download.
Which three Annex A terms the 19 Sep 2025 update added, and which 43 the 17 Aug 2026 update changed: not seen in detail.

Who puts codes on voluntary (MedWatch 3500, MW-numbered) reports: the FDA data-files page says sections E-H are empty for voluntary reports, and I found no statement on whether FDA staff assign codes to them. Unverified.

Current share of MAUDE reports by reporter type: only the older ~95% manufacturer figure (S5). A search snippet mentioned 3.38% non-manufacturer for 1997-2018 and an FDA figure of 93%, but I did not open those sources.
The HHS OIG 2009 report (OEI-01-08-00110) and GAO reports (PEMD-89-10, HEHS-97-21) were seen only as search snippets; the OIG PDF failed on a certificate error.
The 2016 FDA guidance 'Medical Device Reporting for Manufacturers' was not found or read; it may contain more on coding and supplements.
Shi and Gong (Stud Health Technol Inform 2025) could not be found, so the earlier lead stays unverified.
The BMJ 2026 summary-report study and the BMJ 2025 late-reporting study were seen only through press material and snippets.
The method behind Khanal's 26.47% inaccurate codes was not seen.
implications: Treat the key as 'the filer's code'. Report results as agreement with the filing rather than accuracy about what broke, and add level-1 and level-2 agreement next to exact-path agreement, since even an LLM-agreement filter (S14) works at level 2.

Part of the 2025 to 2026 change may come from the code set itself. The 19 Sep 2025 update retired A0202-A0204 and added 3 terms; the 17 Aug 2026 update changed 43 Annex A terms within the test window. Check whether the codes that moved, and the ~3,100 reports per year of changed templates, involve terms touched by these updates, and split 2026 into before and after 17 Aug.

Flag summary malfunction reports (narrative starting 'This report summarizes') and report results with and without them. They are grouped by problem code by design and are a known source of template text with a fixed code.

Because ~95% of reports are manufacturer-filed and coding differs by filer type, check accuracy by manufacturer and hold out by manufacturer: much of the 'skill' may be learning each firm's filing habit.

The LLMs' literal readings (e.g., Failure to Reset vs Pumping Stopped) conflict with the filer's habit, not with any trained coder's ruling. A small human-adjudicated set read by a domain expert would be the only way to say who is right; at present nobody has measured this for Annex A.

For the owner: MAUDE is widely used in device-safety research, but using its device-problem code as an ML ground truth is nearly unstudied (one 2026 preprint, which filters the codes). That is both an opening and a reason to describe the label honestly.

Opened How to Code: importers and user facilities use F10, manufacturers use H6, and filers should pick the lowest-level, most detailed code (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/mdr-adverse-event-codes/how-code-mdr-adverse-event-report, current as of 08/21/2026). checks.claim: About 95% of MAUDE reports come from manufacturers; Ensign and Cohen put user facilities, voluntary reporters and distributors together at about 5%.
checks.detail: Opened PMC5994953 (Ensign LG, Cohen KB, eGEMs 2017;5(1):12, doi:10.5334/egems.221). Under Data Availability, roughly 5 percent of reports come from user facilities, voluntary submitters (health professionals, consumers) and distributors; the Background says the vast majority now come from manufacturers. These are older data, and the paper does not print a 95% figure; that number is an inference.

checks.claim: FDA reviews every report, no FDA document says it re-codes, and Ensign and Cohen say the code field is not checked on entry.
checks.detail: The MAUDE page and the MDR page say FDA reviews all MDRs (the MDR page also says over two million a year, current 03/27/2025: https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/medical-device-safety/medical-device-reporting-mdr-how-report-medical-device-problems). Neither page describes re-coding. Ensign and Cohen, Technical Tips: 'the DEVICE PROBLEM CODE field is not verified upon entry', and filers can enter codes for products other than the one reported.

checks.claim: A report may carry several codes but not a parent together with its child, and at least one code of each required type is mandatory.
checks.detail: How to Code: F10 needs at least one A, G, E and F code; H6 needs those plus B, C and D. Several codes are allowed, and filers should not select both a parent and its child. The MDR codes page puts this as 'don't need both'. I did not reopen S11, the 2009 archive page.

checks.claim: Follow-up reports can change the record: supplements are due within 30 days of new information, placeholder codes are replaced after investigation, and MAUDE shows only the latest information.
checks.detail: The MAUDE page does say FDA displays the most recent MDR information. Its field table also says, for Medical Device Problem Code, that additional information in follow-up reports is 'added to previously cited device problems'. So follow-up codes are appended, not substituted, and a report's code list can grow over time. The placeholder codes on How to Code (4118, 3233, 11) are for the investigation types B, C and D, not the Annex A device-problem code. I did not reopen 21 CFR 803.56.

checks.claim: A24-A27 are catch-all terms, and Annex A reflects the problem as complained rather than the investigated cause.
checks.detail: This rests only on the Emergo industry article (S17), which I did not reopen, and the IMDRF site was not read. Indirect support: the BMJ 2026 abstract (Europe PMC) quotes the device-problem code values 'adverse event without identified device or use problem' and 'insufficient information'.

checks.claim: The code set changes every year: 19 Sep 2025 added 3 Annex A terms, modified 16 and retired A0202-A0204; 17 Aug 2026 modified 43.
checks.detail: Opened https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/mdr-adverse-event-codes/coding-resources-medical-device-reports (current 08/20/2026). 2025 added A0416, A072203 and A150106, modified 16, retired A0202-A0204. 2026 modified 43, none added. Earlier entries match: 2024 +6/4, 2023 +4/4 with A071205 retired, 2022 +9/6, 2021 2 modified. The 2020-21 move to IMDRF rests on snippets only (S19) and was not checked.

checks.claim: Since 2018, summary malfunction reports are grouped by brand x model x problem code and must open with 'This report summarizes XXX malfunction events'.
checks.detail: Opened the GovInfo FR 2018-17770 notice and the FDA VMSR page (current 03/27/2025). Both say one report per unique combination of brand, model and problem code(s), filed quarterly, with the B5 opening sentence fixed. However, the BMJ 2026 study counts only 6,308 summary reports in MAUDE over Jul 2019 - Jun 2025, so this mechanism explains very little of the corpus. Most of these reports also carry A24 or A26, which the project's filter removes.

checks.claim: Coding differs strongly by type of filer (Mishali et al. 2025).
checks.detail: Opened the abstract at https://cris.haifa.ac.il/en/publications/understanding-variation-among-medical-device-reporting-sources-a-/; Crossref confirms doi:10.1016/j.clinthera.2024.10.004, Clin Ther 47(1):76-81. Codes were grouped by hand. Manufacturers: device 36.3%, unknown 32%, clinical 19.3%. User facilities: device 54.3%, use 30.8%, unknown 11.4%. Distributors: clinical 85.7%. P<0.00001. This shows the code mix differs by reporter. It does not show different coding of the same event, since different reporters file different events.

checks.claim: One dissertation judged 26.47% of 102 sampled codes inaccurate.
checks.detail: doi:10.7282/T3TX3JPK resolves (302) to https://rucore.libraries.rutgers.edu/rutgers-lib/56984; I opened the abstract. Khanal D, Rutgers PhD 2018: 102 computing-related events (2007-2016), 62.74% missing codes, 26.47% inaccurate codes. The abstract does not say how accuracy was judged. It concludes the codes should not be used in research for that purpose.

checks.claim: BMJ 2026: 57% of summary reports name no device or use problem, 38% insufficient information.
checks.detail: Read the abstract via Europe PMC (DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100812; Zhou A, Kinard M, Tingley S, Redberg RF; BMJ 2026;395:e100812, published 14 Oct 2026) and the press release. The 57% is reports with the device-problem code 'adverse event without identified device or use problem'. The 38% is reports that 'selected insufficient information' in the device-problem code field. These are code findings, which is stronger than the report's wording. The abstract also gives 11% wrongly marked non-summary, 7% listed n=1, and 55% late. The report's source S15 was the press release only.

checks.claim: No FDA, GAO or HHS OIG audit of coding accuracy was found.
checks.detail: An absence claim. My own searches also found no regulator audit of problem-code accuracy.

checks.claim: Nobody has measured inter-rater reliability of IMDRF Annex A coding.
checks.detail: There is no kappa study on MAUDE narratives, but two studies come close and both were missed. (1) Choi SJ et al., BMC Health Serv Res 2024;24 (doi:10.1186/s12913-024-11885-1). I read the abstract via Europe PMC, PMC11562707. In an online survey of 72 regulatory-training participants coding six virtual cases, most chose broad level-1 codes, code choice varied widely (case 1), and just over 50% chose the intended codes even in case 6. (2) Li H et al., npj Digit Med 2026 (doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02353-7; I opened PMC12992660). Two human annotators judging LLM-versus-vendor device-problem codes agreed with each other 76% of the time.

checks.claim: Using MAUDE device-problem codes as an ML answer key is rare; the only study found (Muaz et al. 2026) keeps 1,728 of 2,899 records where an LLM agrees at level 2.
checks.detail: I opened and parsed https://eprints.dkit.ie/1049/1/maudepreproc-aiai26-preprint.pdf (Muaz M, Janjua ZH, Loughran R, St John Lynch N; 26 Apr 2026). Confirmed: manufacturers code the reports; Gemini Flash 3 agreement at Level 2 keeps 2,899 -> 1,728 (Annex A) and 2,899 -> 1,224 (E/F), i.e. 40% and 58% dropped; the drops are attributed mainly to hedged manufacturer language plus some coding errors; GPT-OSS-120B scores 59.49% at L1 and 23.04% at L3. Also: the 2,899 came from a 10,000-record sample. 'The only such study' is wrong. Li et al. npj Digit Med 2026 had an LLM re-code device-problem codes (IMDRF Annex A) on 1,841 MDRs and compared them with vendor codes, using blinded human adjudication.

bad_sources: S5 is cited as 'Ensign LG, Cohen KB ... eGEMs 2017' without volume or DOI. The correct citation is EGEMS (Wash DC) 2017;5(1):12, doi:10.5334/egems.221. The content claims check out, but '~95% manufacturer' is an inference, not a printed figure, and the data are pre-2017.

S15 is cited as the press release. The abstract is available via Europe PMC (Zhou, Kinard, Tingley, Redberg, BMJ 2026;395:e100812) and should be the cited source. The press release understates that the 57% and 38% are device-problem code values.

Gap 7 says Shi and Gong (Stud Health Technol Inform 2025) 'could not be found'. It exists: Shi Y, Yang E, Gong Y, 'Unveiling Endoscopic Procedures in MAUDE: An ETL-LLM Method', Stud Health Technol Inform 328, 2025, doi:10.3233/SHTI250680. I checked it on Crossref and Europe PMC; it is reference [16] of Muaz et al. It is an ETL+LLM extraction study for endoscopic clips, not a problem-code classifier.
S3 is used for 'placeholder codes are replaced after investigation' as if this concerned the device-problem code. The page's placeholders (4118, 3233, 11) are investigation codes of types B, C and D.

S19 and S20 are snippet-only and should not carry the '2020-21 switch' and the 'IMDRF Release 2026 0 added / 43 modified, 380 requests' details. The 43-modified figure is independently confirmed on the FDA S4 page.
corrections: 'MAUDE shows only the latest version' is incomplete. FDA's MAUDE page says device-problem codes from follow-up reports are added to the codes already cited, not substituted. A report's code list can grow over time, which matters for the project's 'exactly one informative code' filter, and a single-code report may later become multi-code.

'Nobody has measured how well trained coders agree on Annex A codes' is too strong. Choi et al. 2024 (BMC HSR) measured code-choice variation among 72 trained participants on six virtual cases: most chose level-1 codes, and choices were diverse. Li et al. 2026 (npj Digit Med) reports 76% agreement between two human annotators judging device-problem codes. Neither is a kappa on MAUDE narratives.

'The only such study (Muaz et al. 2026)' is wrong. Li H, He X, Subbaswamy A, Vossler P, Gossmann A, Singh K, Feng J, npj Digit Med 2026 (doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02353-7) used an LLM to re-code event type and IMDRF Annex A device-problem codes on 1,841 MDRs. Where the LLM and the vendor code disagreed, blinded human annotators preferred the LLM's device-problem code in 74% of non-tied cases (60.8 vs 21.7). The paper describes vendor codes as varying with the coder's perspective and as sometimes misaligned with the text. This closely mirrors the project's own blinded-reader result (35/40 for the LLM).

The BMJ 2026 figures are device-problem code results: 57% of summary reports carry 'adverse event without identified device or use problem' and 38% 'insufficient information'. The source is the abstract via Europe PMC; authors Zhou, Kinard, Tingley, Redberg.

Summary malfunction reports are a minor mechanism for this corpus. BMJ 2026 counts only 6,308 of them over six years, against over two million MDRs a year, and most carry A24 or A26, which the project already filters out. The habitual template text in the project's pools must come mainly from ordinary individual manufacturer reports.

Mishali et al. show that the mix of code categories differs by reporter type. That does not show that different filers code the same event differently, so 'coding differs strongly by filer' overstates it.
The '32% of reports carry a code' and '~5% non-manufacturer' figures from Ensign and Cohen describe older MAUDE files. Today H6 and F10 require at least one code of each type.
Muaz et al.'s 2,899 records were themselves a pre-processed subset of a 10,000-record sample. The study did not use full MAUDE.

check.net: The device-problem code on a MAUDE report is whatever the filer entered: H6 for manufacturers, who file the vast majority of reports, and F10 for importers and user facilities. FDA asks for the most specific fitting code. FDA says it reviews all reports but publishes nothing about re-coding them, and Ensign and Cohen note that the field is not verified on entry. Follow-up reports add codes to the earlier ones rather than replacing them, and the Annex A code set itself changes every year; on 17 Aug 2026 FDA updated 43 terms, inside the project's test window. Evidence that the filed codes are unreliable is limited but consistent. A small dissertation judged 26% of sampled codes inaccurate. BMJ 2026 found that most summary reports carry catch-all codes, although summary reports are rare and are mostly filtered out by the project. Trained regulators coding the same virtual cases chose diverse, mostly level-1 codes (Choi et al. 2024). The report missed the strongest source, Li et al. (npj Digit Med 2026). In that study an LLM re-coded Annex A device-problem codes for 1,841 MDRs, and on disagreements blinded human annotators preferred the LLM's code in 74% of non-tied cases; the two annotators agreed with each other only 76% of the time. That matches the project's own blinded-reader result. MAUDE itself is very widely used, with 523 PubMed studies by 2022, but using its filed device-problem code as an ML answer key is rare. The two LLM studies that do so (Muaz et al. 2026; Li et al. 2026) both treat the filed code as noisy rather than as ground truth. So the key is best described as the filer's habitual, legally required classification, not an expert judgment of what failed. 'Wrong' overstates it, but treating it as truth is not supported, and agreement with it should be reported as agreement with the filing.

lit.title: What is known, with numbers, about how accurate or consistent MAUDE coded fields are?

report.answer: Short version: nobody has measured how often a MAUDE device-problem code matches the code an expert would pick from the narrative. I found no study that had trained people re-read narratives and score the filed device-problem code. What the literature does measure points one way: the coded fields are unreliable in places. The best-documented errors are in the event-type field. Among reports in which the narrative says the patient died, 23% (95% CI 20-25%) were not filed as deaths, and 17% of all deaths sit under other categories (Lalani et al., JAMA IM 2021, 1,000 reports read by one of two authors). For two heart-valve devices the shares were 17.5% and 24.7% (Meier et al. 2019). In summary reports the device-problem field is mostly vague: 57% say 'adverse event without identified device or use problem' and 38% say 'insufficient information' (Zhou et al., BMJ 2026, 6,308 reports). Codes also vary by who files: manufacturers, distributors and hospitals choose very different code categories. When 72 people trained in IMDRF coding coded six invented cases, most picked broad level-1 codes, and the intended Annex A code was rarely chosen (Choi et al. 2024). The nearest thing to our question is a 2026 preprint (Muaz et al.). An LLM and the filed code agreed at IMDRF level 2 on only 1,728 of 2,899 device-problem records (about 60%). The authors put most of the gap down to vague manufacturer wording and only a smaller part to human coding errors, but no expert checked which side was right. That roughly 60% sits close to our own Opus zero-shot agreement of 54% at level 2. As for 'does everyone use it': MAUDE is very widely used, with 523 PubMed articles by August 2022 (Li et al., J Patient Saf 2024). But almost all of them count codes or read narratives by hand for one device. Hardly anyone treats the filed device-problem code as a gold-standard answer key for automatic coding, and the one benchmark corpus I found (Wunnava et al. 2024) wrote its own annotations because the structured fields miss information.

gaps: No study of device-problem code accuracy against an expert reading of the narrative, for any device, in MAUDE.

No kappa or percent-agreement study for IMDRF Annex A coding, in the US or by EU/UK/Canada/Australia/Japan regulators. The Japanese studies I saw (Yagahara 2025) are about translation mapping, not coding agreement.
No study comparing manufacturers on matched events; the evidence is only indirect.

No MAUDE-specific measured duplicate rate. Individual studies remove duplicates (for example, 39 of 191 device-relevant reports in the ureteroscope study), and a figure for FAERS (drugs) appeared only in a search snippet.
The BMJ 2026 summary-report study (S3) and the BMJ 2025 late-reporting study (S4) were read as abstracts only.
Choi 2024 (S6) Table 2 percentages were read through a summarising fetch and the paper's denominators are inconsistent, so treat the 2-11% figure as approximate.
The MD+DI 2016 article on deaths filed as injuries (Device Events / Madris Tomes) returned HTTP 403, so it is unverified.
The 2023 IMDRF AET WG update slides timed out, so I could not check whether IMDRF has run an internal coding-consistency exercise.
implications: The answer to 'are the labels themselves wrong?' is: partly, and in a known direction. The filed code is the manufacturer's choice, often habitual, and nobody has validated it against an expert reading. Our own numbers (Opus 54% agreement at level 2, a 2026 drift of about 3,100 reports a year to sibling codes) fit this picture, and the one comparable external figure (about 60% LLM-to-filed agreement at level 2, S7) is in the same range.

In the paper, the target can be named honestly as 'the code the manufacturer filed', which is what the FDA and analysts actually use, rather than 'the true device problem'. The accuracy numbers then measure how well a method reproduces filing practice.

Our 3-agent blinded reading (preferring the LLM on 35/40 ordinary disagreements) is not an expert adjudication. A small human-expert adjudication of disagreements would be a first in the literature for device-problem codes, since nobody has measured this. If done, report agreement by tree level, because the literature shows coders diverge mostly below level 1.

MAUDE is widely used (523+ papers) but almost never as a gold-standard answer key for automatic coding, so the project is not reusing a benchmark everyone trusts. It should say so plainly and cite the event-type (S1, S2) and summary-report (S3) error studies as the established evidence that coded fields are imperfect.

Reporter-type and manufacturer effects (S5, S10) support stratifying results by manufacturer and template, which matches our finding that template copying alone is right 96.5% of the time on repeated texts.

S16 is slightly misquoted: the source says 'more than 60 percent' of old codes fit, not 'only about 60%'.
S8 does not support the claim that almost all MAUDE papers count codes or read narratives by hand; it only reports query reproducibility.
corrections: Lalani 2021: the 23% (95% CI 20-25%) is the share of NLP-flagged reports filed as injury, malfunction, other or missing that actually described a death (about 31,552 of 138,996). The figure that answers 'what share of deaths were misfiled' is 17% (16-19%).

Muaz et al. 2026: the about 60% (1,728/2,899) level-2 agreement is with Gemini Flash 3. It was computed after vague codes had been removed, allowed several codes per report, and counted same-parent or ancestor pairs as agreement. It is a more lenient measure and cannot be set side by side with our single-code 54% at level 2. Its 'mostly manufacturer language, smaller part coding error' split is the authors' assertion, not a measurement.

The claim that nobody has measured code accuracy is too strong. Khanal's 2018 Rutgers dissertation reports problem codes missing in 62.74% and inaccurate in 26.47% of 102 sampled computing-related events (abstract only; method unclear). The statement should be: no peer-reviewed study has measured it, and one small dissertation sample found codes often missing or inaccurate.
Everhart 2025: the 54.8% of late reports is attributed to 3 manufacturers and 13 devices together.
S16: 'more than 60 percent' of legacy codes fit the new hierarchy.

The answer to 'is this the data everyone uses?' should separate two things. MAUDE is very widely used: 523 PubMed papers by Aug 2022 per Li 2024. Using the filed device-problem code as an answer key for automatic coding is rare, and S8 does not show that most MAUDE papers are descriptive counts; that part is the checker's and the report's impression, not a measured fact.
Several sources (Everhart, Benham, Mishali Digit Health, Kavanagh) are about timeliness or reporting volume, not code accuracy. They should not be counted as evidence that the labels are wrong.
missed: Khanal D. Analyses of medical device failures related to computing technology. PhD dissertation, Rutgers University, 2018 (https://rucore.libraries.rutgers.edu/rutgers-lib/56984/, abstract only). In 102 sampled computing-related MAUDE events, problem codes were missing in 62.74% and inaccurate in 26.47%; the author says the codes should not be used in research. This is the closest thing to a direct accuracy measurement of MAUDE problem codes.

Shi Y, Gong Y. Leveraging LLMs to Understand Narratives in MAUDE Reports. Stud Health Technol Inform 2025;323:194-198, doi 10.3233/SHTI250076 (opened via https://ebooks.iospress.nl/pdf/doi/10.3233/SHTI250076; content summarised by the fetch). GPT-4-turbo reads endoscopic-clip narratives for uncoded procedures. It reports no agreement with the filed device-problem codes, so it does not measure label accuracy. It was the earlier lead and should be listed as such.

FDA 'About MAUDE' page (opened, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/mandatory-reporting-requirements-manufacturers-importers-and-device-user-facilities/about-manufacturer-and-user-facility-device-experience-maude-database). It says submitters are asked to enter the codes that most accurately describe the problem, lists 'inaccuracies in reports' as a limitation, and says MAUDE shows the latest follow-up version of a report. That last point matters for which code a pool holds.

Ensign LG, Cohen KB. A primer to the structure, content and linkage of the FDA's MAUDE files. eGEMs 2017 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5994953; seen only as a search snippet, not opened). It is a standard reference on how naive joins of the device-problem files cause errors, and the paper's data section should cite it once read.
check.net: No peer-reviewed study has had experts re-read MAUDE narratives and scored the filed device-problem code. The only direct figure I found is a 2018 Rutgers dissertation: in 102 computing-related events, codes were missing in 63% and inaccurate in 26%. It is a small, specific sample, and the method was visible only from the abstract. The best-documented errors are in other coded fields. In Lalani 2021, about 17% of deaths were filed under other categories, and 23% of the NLP-flagged non-death reports in fact described a death. Meier 2019 found 17.5% and 24.7% of deaths misfiled for two heart valves. Summary reports mostly carry vague device-problem codes (57% 'no identified problem', 38% 'insufficient information'; Zhou 2026). Codes are chosen by the reporter, mostly the manufacturer (96.6% of reports), and FDA describes no re-coding step. Who files changes which code categories are used (Mishali 2025). Trained people coding invented cases with IMDRF terms rarely chose the intended Annex A code (2-11%; Choi 2024). The nearest machine-learning study (Muaz et al. 2026) found about 60% filed-code/Gemini agreement at level 2. That measure was more lenient than ours and had no adjudication, so it is consistent with our 54% but not directly comparable. MAUDE itself is very widely used (523 PubMed papers by 2022). Using the filed device-problem code as the answer key for automatic coding is uncommon, so this project is not reusing a trusted benchmark. The honest name for the target is 'the code the reporter filed'.

lit.title: Who uses MAUDE, for what, and is narrative-to-device-problem-code an established ML task with a shared benchmark?

report.answer: MAUDE is widely used, but almost never as a machine-learning benchmark. PubMed has 913 records with "MAUDE" or "Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience" in the title or abstract. The yearly count rose from 21 in 2015 to 105 in 2024, 107 in 2025 and 132 so far in 2026. Nearly all of these are clinical, device-specific descriptive studies that pull reports for one device and count event types or filed problem codes. Only 31 of the 913 mention ML, NLP, BERT, LLMs or text mining. Most of those use the authors' own labels for a different task: health-IT event or not (Chai 2013; Kang & Gong 2020; Luschi 2023), ML-device events (Wang 2024), harm or no harm (da Vinci, 2024), severity, or LLM extraction of complications for one device (SpaceOAR, endoscopic clips). I found only two published set-ups that predict the filed device-problem code from the narrative. (1) MADE (Agarwal et al., Fraunhofer HHI, arXiv 2604.15203, ACL 2026) is a public benchmark (Hugging Face, MIT licence, gated). It covers 2015 to mid-2025, splits train/validation/test by time (2015-2023 / Jan-Jun 2024 / Jul 2024-Jun 2025), deduplicates on the event description, and maps FDA terms to IMDRF. It is multi-label, combining product and patient problems: 1,154 labels, 8.79 per report, 488,273 reports. The best macro-F1 is 0.54 (Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned; GPT-5 with 10 kNN examples), and the rarest labels reach only 0.12-0.34. (2) Muaz et al. (AIAI 2026) took 10,000 random 2016-2025 reports. They removed the Insufficient Information and no-problem codes, mapped FDA codes to IMDRF (2,899 left), and then kept only the 1,728 records where Gemini Flash 3 agreed with the filed code at level 2. On that pre-filtered set, zero-shot GPT-OSS-120B matched device-problem codes at 0.59 (level 1) and 0.36 (level 3). The abstract's "23.04% at Level 3" is the patient-problem figure in their Table 1, not the device-problem one. Both papers say outright that the filed codes are unverified and may be noisy. MADE says inter-annotator agreement has never been assessed. Muaz et al. built their set specifically to filter out records whose code they did not trust. The FDA's own MAUDE pages say the submitter chooses the codes and that reports may be inaccurate and unverified. I found no published FDA NLP model for MAUDE coding, and no leaderboard. In short, the project's set-up is unusual but not new. A temporal split, filed codes as labels, IMDRF mapping and a long tail are all familiar from MADE. Restricting to single-code reports, scoring the exact leaf code, keeping natural proportions and copying templates by digit-masked deduplication is a combination nobody has published. Whether the filed code is the truth is an open question that the field has named but not measured.

gaps: Full text of Shi & Gong 2025 (SHTI250076) is behind a subscription; only the abstract was read, so its sample size and any evaluation figures are unknown.
The Khanal 2018 dissertation's method for judging problem codes 'inaccurate' was not visible on the landing page.
The FDA's MedWatch MDR code instructions (how many codes may be chosen, whether to pick the most specific) were not opened.
Whether the Wunnava et al. 935-report corpus was ever released was not confirmed.
The MADE appendix was read through WebFetch summaries; exact field names and the up-propagation details of the HF release were not inspected (the dataset is gated).
The Elsa/FDA internal AI claims come from secondary sources only; no FDA primary document on AI for MAUDE coding was found.

PubMed counts use title/abstract matching and will miss papers that mention MAUDE only in the full text, and include a few non-device 'Maude' hits; OpenAlex counts were not tabulated by year because the term 'Maude' collides with the Maude programming language.
IEEE Xplore, AMIA proceedings beyond PubMed, Kaggle and Drug Safety were not searched directly; coverage there rests on web and OpenAlex searches.
The MAUDE-Atlas dataset (OSF/Zenodo, commercial) was seen only as an abstract; its benchmark contents were not checked.
implications: To the owner's question 'is everyone using this?': yes, MAUDE is used by about 100+ papers a year, but almost all are clinical descriptive studies, not ML. Narrative-to-device-problem-code is not an established ML task. There is one public benchmark (MADE, 2026) and one small LLM study (Muaz, 2026).

To 'aren't the labels wrong?': the field already treats filed codes as unverified, submitter-chosen labels. MADE says so in its limitations; Muaz et al. discard about 40% of records whose code an LLM does not confirm; the FDA itself makes no claim of verification. The project's finding that the filed code tracks the manufacturer's template habit rather than a literal reading fits this. It is also more specific than anything published: 35.2% of single-code reports share text filed under more than one code, and copying the code of an earlier identical report covers 64.8% of reports and is right 96.5% of the time. Nobody has measured that.

Cite MADE as the closest published set-up and contrast with it explicitly: single-code vs multi-label, device problems only vs product plus patient, natural proportions vs HDBSCAN downsampling, exact leaf vs propagated hierarchy, and copying identical templates vs first-occurrence deduplication. MADE's long-tail numbers (extreme-tail F1 0.12-0.34, GPT-5 better on rare labels and a fine-tuned 8B model better on frequent ones) are the closest external comparison for the rare-code results.

A reviewer who knows MAUDE will find these familiar: the temporal split, filed codes as labels, the IMDRF mapping, removing Insufficient Information / no-problem codes (Muaz did the same), and the long tail. They will question three things: (a) using the filed code as truth without any human adjudication, since all readers so far are LLMs; (b) the single-code restriction, which drops multi-code reports and changes the label distribution relative to MADE; (c) the exact-leaf metric when Muaz and MADE report by tree level.

The project's own numbers sit in the same range as the published zero-shot results. Opus agrees with the filed code on 41% exact / 54% level 2 / 69% level 1. Muaz report GPT-OSS at 0.36 / 0.52 / 0.59 on an easier pre-filtered set, and Gemini agreed at level 2 on about 60% of unfiltered records.

If the paper wants a defensible statement about label quality, the missing piece in the literature is a small human-adjudicated sample: how often an independent expert reading matches the filed code, split by template versus unique narratives. That would be new; no published study has it.
