checks.claim: MADE best macro-F1 0.54; rarest labels reach only 0.12-0.34
checks.detail: Table 2 gives an overall macro-F1 of 0.54 both for Llama-3.1-8B-Base (discriminative, fine-tuned) and for GPT-5 (thinking). Extreme-tail F1 is 0.12 for that Llama model and 0.34 for GPT-5. The best fine-tuned extreme-tail score is 0.16 (Llama-3.1-70B-Base, generative), and across all models extreme-tail F1 falls as low as 0.01 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Kimi-K2). So '0.12-0.34' is the range for the two top models only, not for rare labels in general. Head F1: best fine-tuned 0.74 vs GPT-5 0.68, which supports 'GPT-5 better on rare, fine-tuned better on frequent'. I did not verify that GPT-5 was given 10 kNN examples.

checks.claim: MADE says inter-annotator agreement was never assessed, reports appear single-annotated, some labels come from manufacturers, and also says 'FDA coders assign the IMDRF labels'
checks.detail: The HTML at https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15203v1 contains all of these statements, including the internal tension between 'FDA coders assign' and the note that some labels come from manufacturers.

checks.claim: MADE dataset on Hugging Face: gated, MIT licence, no leaderboard
checks.detail: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ragarwal/MADE-Multilabel-Benchmark: the files are gated behind accepting conditions, the licence is MIT, Table 1 matches the paper, and no leaderboard is described. The card links a project page at Fraunhofer HHI.

Crossref lists the title, the authors Muaz, Janjua, Loughran and St John Lynch, and IFIP AICT / Artificial Intelligence Applications and Innovations, published 2026-07-16. I extracted and read the full preprint text from https://eprints.dkit.ie/1049/1/maudepreproc-aiai26-preprint.pdf.

checks.claim: Muaz: 10,000 random 2016-2025 reports, cleaned and IMDRF-mapped to 2,899; Gemini Flash 3 agreement at level 2 left 1,728 device and 1,224 health-effect records; GPT-OSS-120B device accuracy 0.595/0.523/0.361, patient 0.688/0.555/0.230
checks.detail: Section 3.1 and Table 1 of the preprint give exactly these figures. Records were dropped for redundancy, missing codes, and the Insufficient Information / no identified problem / no appropriate code terms. The authors put the reduction at 40% (device) and 58% (health effect). Scoring is multi-label, and a row counts as correct if any predicted code matches any filed code.

checks.claim: The abstract's '23.04% at Level 3' for device problems is actually the patient-problem figure
checks.detail: The abstract reads '59.49% consensus at Level 1 for device problems and drops to 23.04% at Level 3'. Table 1 gives device L3 = 0.3611 and patient L3 = 0.2304. The Discussion repeats 'as low as 23.04% at Level 3' without naming the category.

checks.claim: Muaz et al. built the set to filter out records whose code they did not trust / discarded ~40% as ambiguous or miscoded
checks.detail: The authors attribute the discarded records mainly to manufacturers' deliberately hedged, non-causal language. Only 'a smaller fraction' is put down to genuine coding errors. They also call the filed codes 'human-annotated' ground truth and present the filter as analogous to filtering on inter-annotator agreement. Their framing is that these records are not reliably codeable, not that the codes are untrusted.

checks.claim: Gemini agreed at level 2 on about 60% of unfiltered records (implication bullet)
checks.detail: The roughly 60% (1,728/2,899) is measured after cleaning, with Insufficient Information and no-problem records already removed, so the records were not 'unfiltered'. It is also a multi-label agreement at level 2 that reconciles codes to a common parent.

checks.claim: Shi & Gong, SHTI 2025;323:194-198, GPT-4-turbo on endoscopic clip narratives to find uncoded surgical procedures; no numbers in abstract
checks.detail: The PubMed efetch abstract for PMID 40200473 and Crossref for doi 10.3233/SHTI250076 confirm the citation and the content. Abstract only.

checks.claim: Wunnava et al. CL4Health 2024: 935 reports, 9 entity types, 12,252 spans; release promised, not found
checks.detail: The abstract page https://aclanthology.org/2024.cl4health-1.29/ confirms the authors, pages 240-245, 935 reports, 12,252 spans, nine entity types, and 'will be made publicly available upon publication' with no link given. I did not verify the inter-annotator precision 0.71 / recall 0.68 or the 822/113 split.

checks.claim: FDA MAUDE page: submitter chooses codes; limitations include inaccurate, unverified reports; no statement that FDA verifies codes
checks.detail: https://www.fda.gov/.../about-manufacturer-and-user-facility-device-experience-maude-database says submitters are asked to enter the codes that most accurately describe the problem. The limitations list passive surveillance, under-reporting, inaccurate reports and unverified causation. The page says FDA reviews MDRs but does not say the codes are verified.

checks.claim: Mishali et al. Clin Ther 2025: manufacturer codes 36.3% device / 32% unknown / 19.3% clinical; distributors 85.7% clinical; user facilities 54.3% device / 30.8% use
checks.detail: The PubMed efetch abstract for PMID 39516116 matches these figures. The DPCs were grouped manually by the authors. Abstract only.

checks.claim: Li et al. J Patient Saf 2024: 523 articles by Aug 2022; 336 with queries; 60 executable; 14 reproducible
checks.detail: The PubMed efetch abstract for PMID 38470959 matches. It shows poor query reproducibility, not that MAUDE studies are mostly query-and-count work, although that reading is reasonable.

checks.claim: Khanal 2018 dissertation: of 102 computing-related events, codes missing 62.74%, inaccurate 26.47%
checks.detail: The landing page https://rucore.libraries.rutgers.edu/rutgers-lib/56984/ confirms the numbers and N=102. The judging method is not shown. Crossref does not resolve doi 10.7282/t3tx3jpk, so I could not check the DOI. Weak evidence, as the report said.

checks.claim: S10 numbers: Chai 2013 (570,272 incidents, 1,534 HIT, 0.297%, F1 0.954); Kang 2020 (6,994, F1 0.876, 0.862 independent); Luschi 2023 (3,075); Wang 2024 (F1 85%); Mao 2022 (F1 91.5%); Yu 2024 (4,459); Sohoni 2026 (1,455); Kesharwani 2026 ('linguistic conventions')
checks.detail: The PubMed efetch abstracts for PMIDs 23666777, 32916305, 37954315, 38269880, 34919294, 39049270, 41565161 and 42174919 contain these figures. In Kang 2020, F1 0.876 is for the hybrid model and 0.862 is the accuracy on the independent dataset. All of these use the authors' own labels; none predicts filed problem codes.

checks.claim: da Vinci BERT-BiLSTM paper attributed to 'Wang et al.?' (Front Comput Neurosci 2024)
checks.detail: Crossref for 10.3389/fncom.2024.1476164 confirms the title, but the first author is Li (authors Li, Zhu, Xia, Wang, Li, Zhang), not Wang. I did not verify the abstract figures (4,568 reports, F1 90.15%).

checks.claim: Other S11 items (biomaterial medRxiv macro-F1 0.925 vs 0.827; PFA adjudication kappa 0.83; stapler IJMDI; cochlear 74.8-88.6%; MAUDE-Atlas)
checks.detail: Not opened in this check. The cochlear-implant ML paper exists (medRxiv 10.1101/2020.04.30.20086660 appeared in my search results), but I did not verify its numbers.

checks.claim: No FDA-authored NLP model for MAUDE coding; Jiang et al. Foot Ankle Int 2023 used text mining plus manual review
checks.detail: The PubMed abstract for PMID 36461676 confirms that FDA OPEQ authors applied text mining followed by manual review. The absence of an FDA coding model is an absence finding and I cannot prove it. The Elsa claims rest on snippets only.

checks.claim: Nobody has measured how often filed device-problem codes match an independent expert reading across device types
checks.detail: My searches also found no such measurement for device-problem codes. They did find published measurements of misclassification in another MAUDE coded field, the reporter-chosen event type (death vs injury/malfunction). The report missed these (see missed). So 'labels on MAUDE reports are often wrong' has been measured for event type, not for problem codes.

checks.claim: Project numbers comparable: Opus 41/54/69 vs Muaz GPT-OSS 0.36/0.52/0.59
checks.detail: The comparison is loose. Muaz score multi-label any-match on a set pre-filtered for LLM agreement, with the IMDRF Annex A/E/F codes in the prompt, so their numbers are not on the same footing as a single-code exact-path score on natural proportions.

bad_sources: S11 da Vinci paper: first author is Li (Li, Zhu, Xia, Wang, Li, Zhang per Crossref 10.3389/fncom.2024.1476164), not 'Wang et al.'
S14 DOI 10.7282/t3tx3jpk did not resolve in Crossref (the landing page does exist)
S1 ML subset: several of the '31' hits are not ML work, and one (PMID 40105162) is not MAUDE data at all (Bosnian inspection data, with an expression of concern)
corrections: MADE extreme-tail F1 '0.12-0.34' is the range for the two top models only (Llama-3.1-8B-Base 0.12, GPT-5 0.34). The best fine-tuned model reaches 0.16, and some models score 0.01. All MADE scores are on a 10,288-report stratified 'truncated test set', not on the full 118,177 test split.

Muaz et al. attribute the 40% (device) / 58% (health effect) discard mainly to manufacturers' hedged, non-causal language, and only a smaller fraction to coding errors. They treat the filed codes as 'human-annotated' ground truth. Do not say they discarded records as 'miscoded'.

The roughly 60% Gemini level-2 agreement in Muaz is on already-cleaned records (Insufficient Information and no-problem codes removed, IMDRF-mapped), under multi-label any-match. It is not 'unfiltered'.

The comparison between the project's 41/54/69 and Muaz's 0.36/0.52/0.59 is not like for like. Muaz use multi-label any-match on an LLM-agreement-filtered set; the project uses single code, exact path, natural proportions.
The ML subset count depends on the query (I got 32), and it includes non-ML and non-MAUDE papers. ML on MAUDE narratives is an even smaller niche than '31 of 913' suggests.

The 'nobody measured' finding should be narrowed. Nobody has measured the accuracy of device-problem codes against independent expert reading. Misclassification of another reporter-chosen field (event type) has been measured in JAMA Intern Med papers.
missed: Lalani C, Kunwar EM, Kinard M, Dhruva SS, Redberg RF. JAMA Intern Med 2021;181(9):1217-1223 (PMID 34309624, doi 10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.3942). Abstract read via PubMed efetch. NLP search plus manual review of MAUDE 1991-2020: about 23% of reports whose narrative said the patient died were filed as injury/malfunction/other, and about 17% of deaths were classified in other categories. This is direct evidence that a reporter-chosen coded field on MAUDE is often inconsistent with the narrative. URL: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=34309624&rettype=abstract

Meier, Wang, Tomes, Redberg, JAMA Intern Med 2019 research letter (Sapien 3 / MitraClip). Search snippet only: 217 of 1,238 Sapien 3 deaths and 97 of 392 MitraClip deaths were filed as injury/malfunction. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2752362 (snippet only; verify before citing)

BMJ 2026 cross-sectional study of MAUDE summary reports, July 2019 - June 2025 (doi 10.1136/bmj-2026-100812, per the BMJ press release I opened). Of 6,308 summary reports, 57% gave no device or use problem and 38% insufficient information. This shows manufacturer coding defaults to the uninformative codes at scale. https://bmjgroup.com/medical-device-adverse-event-reports-are-often-incomplete-inaccurate-and-delayed/ (press release only)

In the Muaz preprint, the authors explicitly describe MAUDE narratives as written by manufacturers' regulatory staff in deliberately hedged, non-attributing language. This bears directly on the project's template-habit finding and is citable from the full text (https://eprints.dkit.ie/1049/1/maudepreproc-aiai26-preprint.pdf, Section 3.1).
check.net: MAUDE is heavily used: PubMed has 913 title/abstract records, rising to 105-132 a year in 2024-2026. Almost all of these are device-specific descriptive studies, and their queries are often not reproducible (Li et al. 2024: 14 of 60 executable queries reproduced). Predicting the filed device-problem code from the narrative is not an established ML task. The only public benchmark is MADE (ACL 2026), which is multi-label over product and patient problems mapped to IMDRF (1,154 labels) with a temporal split. It is evaluated on a 10,288-report truncated test set, and the best overall macro-F1 is 0.54. Extreme-tail F1 is 0.34 for GPT-5 but at most 0.16 for fine-tuned models, and MADE has no leaderboard. Muaz et al. (AIAI 2026) is a small zero-shot study on a set kept only where Gemini agreed with the filed code at level 2. Its abstract's '23.04% at Level 3' is the patient-problem figure; device-problem level 3 is 0.36. On whether the labels are wrong: the FDA says submitters choose the codes and makes no claim to verify them. MADE says label agreement was never assessed. Muaz attribute unclear records mainly to manufacturers' deliberately hedged language. Published studies have measured misclassification of a different reporter-chosen field, death recorded as injury or malfunction (about 17-23% in Lalani et al. 2021), and code choice differs sharply by reporter type (Mishali 2025). Nobody has published how often the filed device-problem code matches an independent expert reading of the narrative. The project's template-habit numbers are therefore new, but they should be framed as filing consistency, not as proof that the codes are wrong.

lit.title: Where the answer key is an administrative code chosen by the filer: how wrong is it known to be, and what do researchers do?

report.answer:
Yes, partly, and every neighbouring field has found the same thing. When whoever files a record also picks its code, that code is often not what a careful expert re-reader would choose. The mismatch is mostly systematic: the same filer makes the same habitual choice, often a generic parent where the text supports a specific child. It is rarely random noise.

Measured sizes vary by field:
- **Clinical ICD coding:** a review of 32 UK studies found a median accuracy of 83.2% (IQR 67.3–92.1%) [S5]. Two certified coders re-coding 508 MIMIC-III discharge summaries matched the hospital's own codes with a micro-Jaccard of only 10.7% [S3]. In the MDACE re-coding, professional coders agreed on only about 45% of the MIMIC codes [S2].
- **Radiology ICD-10:** original coders agreed with two expert validators on 65% of notes [S6]. A model's mean average precision (MAP) fell from 88.5% to 48.1% when it was scored against the validated codes instead of the filed ones [S6].
- **CWE labels in the vulnerability database:** 49.7% match exactly, 31.4% are defensible alternatives and 3.6% are clearly wrong. Quality depends most on the organisation that filed the label, with a roughly 70-point spread [S10].
- **MedDRA (drug adverse-event terms):** Norwegian coders reproduced the standard term selection in only 36% of answers [S7]. Yet VAERS staff codes were judged correct on 93.4% of 1,000 symptoms [S9].
- **MAUDE's own event-type field:** reporters filed 23% of reports that describe a death under a category other than death [S12].

There are documented cases where the model was right more often than the key. In Danish hospital coding, expert review found the model right in 66–72% of its disagreements with coders on secondary diagnoses [S4]. In ICD-10 radiology, models that copy the coders' habits score worse against expert-validated codes [S6].

What researchers do about it falls into four patterns:
- Most machine-learning papers still treat the filed code as gold and say so in their limitations [S1].
- The better ones add an expert-validated subset. Typical designs: two readers plus a third to settle disagreements; 50 randomly drawn cases per code; or 100–500 items read by 3–5 experts [S4, S6, S10, S16].
- Some score with a graded verdict: exact match / defensible alternative / wrong [S10]. Others score at a higher tree level [S11].
- A few model the filer directly, either with per-annotator confusion matrices [S18, S19] or by keeping a filer's records out of the training set when testing on them [S20].

The closest precedent for MAUDE is CWE labelling of vulnerability reports. There the filer writes both the text and the code, the taxonomy is a hierarchy, most disagreements are parent-vs-child imprecision, and quality tracks the filer. That community's practice: report the three-way verdict on a read sample and treat the filer's identity as a signal of label reliability [S10].

On the second question, "does everyone use this data?": very little machine-learning work uses MAUDE device-problem codes. The one benchmark found keeps only the reports where an LLM agreed with the filed code at tree level 2, which left 1,728 of 2,899 records after cleaning [S11].

sources.citation: Edin J, Junge A, Havtorn JD, Borgholt L, Maistro M, Ruotsalo T, Maaloe L. Automated Medical Coding on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV: A Critical Review and Replicability Study. SIGIR 2023
sources.says: Uses the MIMIC codes as gold standard. Its limitations section says manual coding is error-prone and partly subjective, cites the median accuracy of 83.2% from S5, and suggests evaluation with a human in the loop. The paper does not measure label quality itself.

sources.citation: Cheng H, et al. MDACE: MIMIC Documents Annotated with Code Evidence. ACL 2023
sources.says: Professional coders re-coded 302 inpatient charts from scratch. Two coders on 3 charts: initial Krippendorff alpha 0.53 inpatient and 0.24 professional-fee, rising to 0.97 and 0.96 after review with a supervisor's final call (Table 2). Table 5: only 2,370 of 5,250 MIMIC inpatient codes (45.1%) were agreed; the paper attributes this partly to missing operative notes and changed coding guidelines.

sources.citation: Kim B-H, Ganapathi V. Read, Attend, and Code: Pushing the Limits of Medical Codes Prediction from Clinical Notes by Machines. MLHC 2021 (PMLR 149)
sources.says: Two certified coders coded 508 randomly drawn MIMIC-III test summaries. Against the hospital's codes they reached micro-Jaccard 10.7, micro-precision 47.7 and micro-recall 12.1 (Table 1). The model scored higher against the same codes (micro-Jaccard 42.0). Footnote 2 says neither set of codes is absolute truth.

sources.citation: Edin J, Butt Balaganeshan S, Kristensen AK, Maaloe L, Louloudis I, Brunak S. A medical coding language model trained on clinical narratives from a population-wide cohort of 1.8 million patients. arXiv 2603.00221v2, 2026 (preprint)
sources.says: Danish ICD-10 coding. For secondary diagnoses where model and coders often disagreed, review of 50 randomly sampled model-only cases per condition found explicit evidence in the note in 76% (weight disorders) and 74% (hypertension). For unspecified-versus-typed diabetes, 74% of sampled cases named the type explicitly. The abstract says the model was correct 66-72% of the time; the conclusion says 76-86%, so the paper is internally inconsistent. Authors attribute the omissions to reimbursement incentives.

sources.citation: Burns EM, et al. Systematic review of discharge coding accuracy. J Public Health (Oxf) 2012. doi:10.1093/pubmed/fdr054
sources.says: 32 UK studies. Median accuracy of routine codes against case notes was 83.2% (IQR 67.3-92.1%), ranging from 50.5% to 97.8% across studies. Primary-diagnosis accuracy rose from 73.8% to 96.0% after Payment by Results was introduced.

sources.citation: Kim Y, Li C, Ye B, Tahmasebi A, Aslam J. Supervised Learning in the Presence of Noise: Application in ICD-10 Code Classification. arXiv 2103.07808, 2021
sources.says: 29,826 radiology notes from several sites, sampled by stratum. Each was reviewed by two or more expert coders, with a third, more experienced coder settling disagreements. Original-vs-validator agreement on the exact code set was 65%; validator-vs-validator 72% (validators could see the original codes). 67% of code replacements cross a chapter or category boundary; symptom (R-chapter) codes are over-used. Model MAP was 88.5% against original labels and 48.1% against validated labels. The authors call the noise systematic: methods that mimic the coders score well on original labels and badly on validated ones.

sources.citation: Norwegian MedDRA coding consistency study. Drug Safety 2025;48(11). doi:10.1007/s40264-025-01573-2 (PMC12515201)
sources.says: 26 public-sector pharmacovigilance coders on 11 ambiguous verbatim terms (286 answers). 36% matched the standard selection exactly; per-task match ranged from 0% to 100%. Of substituted terms, 65.8% stayed within the same High Level Term (one level up in MedDRA), 23.7% moved to another High Level Term in the same System Organ Class (top level), and 10.5% changed System Organ Class. Cites Toneatti 2006: a 12% inaccuracy rate in HIV-trial coding, concentrated on difficult verbatims.

sources.citation: Lalani C, Kunwar EM, Kinard M, Dhruva SS, Redberg RF. Reporting of Death in US FDA Medical Device Adverse Event Reports in Categories Other Than Death. JAMA Intern Med 2021. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.3942
sources.says: Language-processing screen of MAUDE, then two authors read the reports by hand (up to 50 per term, plus a random 1,000). 23% (95% CI 20-25%) of reports describing a death were filed as another category; 17% of deaths were missed. The event type is chosen by the reporter, and manufacturers filed 95.9% of the sampled reports.

sources.citation: Kim B, Nakashole N. SYMPTOMIFY: Transforming Symptom Annotations with Language Model Knowledge Harvesting. Findings of EMNLP 2023
sources.says: VAERS symptoms are coded by certified MedDRA coders. A crowd check of 1,000 randomly drawn symptoms (correct if 2 of 3 raters agreed) judged 93.4% correct; rater Fleiss kappa was 0.55 (Section 4.1).

sources.citation: Nong Y, Du Y, Behravan M, Cai H. How Reliable Are NVD CWE Labels? A Large-Scale Semantic Audit with Seclometry. arXiv 2608.21977, 2026 (preprint)
sources.says: Across 15,556 CVEs: 49.70% exact match with the code-grounded label, 31.37% defensible alternatives under taxonomy ambiguity, 3.63% evidence-inconsistent. The audit tool was validated on 100 hand-curated CVEs (85% top-1, 92% ambiguity-aware accuracy). Two authors independently reviewed 564 flagged labels and confirmed 434 as mislabels (kappa 0.87). The filing organisation (CNA, the body that issues the CVE) is the strongest predictor of label quality, with a roughly 70-point spread in exact match. Most differences are imprecision rather than outright error. The CNA often writes both the description and the label.

sources.citation: Muaz M, Loughran R, Janjua ZH, St John Lynch N. A Framework for LLM-Guided and ISO 5338-Aligned Data Engineering in Medical Device Adverse Event Reporting. Preprint (AIAI 2026), DkIT eprints 1049
sources.says: MAUDE codes are entered by manufacturers' regulatory staff. Their benchmark keeps only records where one LLM (Gemini Flash 3) agrees with the filed IMDRF code at Level 2: 10,000 reports become 2,899 after cleaning and 1,728 after the agreement filter. GPT-OSS-120B then matches the kept codes on 59.49% at Level 1 and 23.04% at Level 3. No human validation. The authors call the discarded 40% mostly strategically hedged narratives.

sources.citation: US FDA. About Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) Database
sources.says: Submitters are asked to enter the device-problem codes. The page lists inaccuracies in reports among the system's limitations and says nothing about FDA validating the codes.

sources.citation: Searle T, Ibrahim Z, Dobson R. Experimental Evaluation and Development of a Silver-Standard for the MIMIC-III Clinical Coding Dataset. BioNLP 2020
sources.says: A concept-extraction tool (MedCAT) predicted codes from discharge diagnoses. A PhD student and a qualified clinical coder checked about 1,580-1,588 sampled predictions per set (Cohen kappa 0.85 and 0.80). For the 10 most frequent codes, 0-35% of occurrences were possibly missing; hypertension was 16% (3,312) possibly missing. S1 restates this as 35% of common codes under-coded, which overstates it. Cites UK accuracy of 50-98%.

sources.citation: Ihshaish H, Mayhew P, Zayet TMA, Del Amo A. The record is part of the task: matched-record evaluation of text classifiers across maintenance, safety and recall reporting. arXiv 2609.16267v2, 2026
sources.says: The ASRS primary-problem label is assigned by NASA analysts, who also write the report synopsis. NHTSA recall component codes are assigned by NHTSA from the manufacturer's report, with acknowledged subjectivity. 39% of NHTSA consequence texts are exact duplicates of another campaign's. The paper argues evaluations should report how both the record and the label were produced. No agreement figures.

sources.citation: FAA. SDRS Field Instructions
sources.says: The submitter (operator or repair station) picks the JASC/ATA code from a drop-down list and one to three nature-of-condition codes. No figures on coding quality.

sources.citation: Irvin J, et al. CheXpert: A Large Chest Radiograph Dataset with Uncertainty Labels and Expert Comparison. AAAI 2019
sources.says: Training labels were extracted automatically from reports. Validation: 200 studies labelled by 3 radiologists. Test: 500 studies by consensus of 5 radiologists. A standard design for weak labels plus a small expert set.

sources.citation: Northcutt CG, Athalye A, Mueller J. Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2021
sources.says: At least 3.3% label errors on average across 10 test sets. Candidates were flagged by algorithm and checked by crowd workers, who confirmed about 51%. On corrected test sets, smaller models can overtake larger ones.

sources.citation: Raykar VC, et al. Learning From Crowds. JMLR 11:1297-1322, 2010
sources.says: Jointly evaluates each annotator, estimates the hidden true labels and learns a classifier when no gold standard exists. Beats majority voting.

sources.citation: Tanno R, Saeedi A, Sankaranarayanan S, Alexander DC, Silberman N. Learning From Noisy Labels By Regularized Estimation Of Annotator Confusion. CVPR 2019
sources.says: Learns one confusion matrix per annotator together with the classifier, and works with a single label per item.

sources.citation: Geva M, Goldberg Y, Berant J. Are We Modeling the Task or the Annotator? EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019
sources.says: Models pick up annotator-specific patterns: adding annotator IDs as features helps, and models generalise poorly to unseen annotators. Recommends that test-set annotators be disjoint from training-set annotators.

sources.citation: Song H, Kim M, Park D, Shin Y, Lee J-G. Learning from Noisy Labels with Deep Neural Networks: A Survey. IEEE TNNLS 2022 (arXiv 2007.08199)
sources.says: Separates instance-independent noise (symmetric, asymmetric, pair) from instance-dependent noise, where the chance of a wrong label depends on the input text itself, and notes the latter is little studied. Groups 62 methods into five families: robust architecture, regularisation, robust loss, loss adjustment, sample selection.

sources.citation: Artstein R, Poesio M. Inter-Coder Agreement for Computational Linguistics. Computational Linguistics 34(4), 2008
sources.says: Summarises Krippendorff: three or more independent coders with a written scheme fixed in advance; each category should appear often enough in the sample; alpha 0.8 is the usual minimum and 0.67 allows tentative conclusions. Weighted coefficients can give partial credit in hierarchical tag sets.

sources.citation: Wang Y, Coiera E, Runciman W, Magrabi F. Using multiclass classification to automate the identification of patient safety incident reports by type and severity. BMC Med Inform Decis Mak 2017
sources.says: For incident type the authors did not use the reporters' categories: three experts validated the labels (kappa 0.93). They note reporters may not be experts in classification. No comparison of reporter and expert labels.

sources.citation: Horsky J, et al. Accuracy and Completeness of Clinical Coding Using ICD-10 for Ambulatory Visits. AMIA Annu Symp Proc 2017
sources.says: In a simulation, 23 clinicians coded six standard scenarios. Just over half of the entered codes were appropriate and about a quarter were omitted; omissions were higher for secondary diagnoses.

sources.citation: Kralova et al. 2023, quality of MedDRA coding in COVID-19 vaccine medication-error data (PubMed 37087705)
sources.says: As cited in S7: of about 1,500 reported terms, roughly half were unspecific or split-coded. The PubMed page itself was blocked.

findings.claim: Clinical ICD coding: the codes come from the hospital's professional coders, not from the clinicians who wrote the notes. Re-reads disagree a lot. UK routine data are 83.2% accurate on median (range 50.5-97.8%). Hired coders matched MIMIC codes with micro-Jaccard 10.7%. MDACE coders agreed on 45.1% of MIMIC inpatient codes. Two coders started at alpha 0.53 and reached 0.97 only after adjudication.
findings.support: S5 abstract; S3 Table 1; S2 Tables 2 and 5

findings.claim: The errors in filed codes are systematic, not random. Coders over-use generic symptom codes; 67% of code replacements cross a chapter or category. A model fitted to the filed codes looks excellent against them (MAP 88.5%) and poor against expert-validated codes (48.1%). Copying the filer's habit and being right pull in opposite directions.
findings.support: S6 Sections 2.2-2.3 and Table 6

findings.claim: There are documented cases where the model beat the key. In Danish coding, 50-case random reviews per condition found explicit evidence for the model's extra code in 74-76% of cases; the paper's headline is 66-72% (abstract) or 76-86% (conclusion). The cause was systematic under-coding of secondary diagnoses, which the authors link to reimbursement rules.
findings.support: S4 Sections 2.4 and conclusion

findings.claim: A three-way verdict (exact / defensible alternative / evidence-inconsistent) splits label disagreement into imprecision and true error. For CWE: 49.7% exact, 31.4% defensible, 3.6% wrong. Exact match varies by about 70 points across filing organisations; true errors vary much less.
findings.support: S10 abstract, Section 6.1.3, Table 10

findings.claim: MedDRA coding of drug and vaccine reports: consistency between coders is low on ambiguous verbatims, with 36% exact match to the standard. Two-thirds of substitutions stay within the same High Level Term, i.e. sibling-level drift. On ordinary VAERS symptoms, accuracy is high: 93.4% judged correct by crowd raters with kappa 0.55.
findings.support: S7 Results and Table 5; S9 Section 4.1

findings.claim: In MAUDE itself, a reporter-chosen field was audited by hand. 23% of reports that describe a death were not filed as deaths, and manufacturers chose the category on more than 95% of reports. No published study audits MAUDE device-problem codes the same way.
findings.support: S8 abstract and methods; S11 Section on LLM-agreement

findings.claim: The only MAUDE coding benchmark found handles label doubt by keeping records where one LLM agrees with the filed code at Level 2. This removes the hard cases by construction, and the filter uses the same kind of reader that is being evaluated. No human validated the codes.
findings.support: S11 Sections 3 and 4

findings.claim: Common practice in ICD machine-learning work is still to accept the filed code as gold and list its errors as a limitation. Some groups add an expert subset (MDACE) or a silver standard checked by hand (Searle: two validators, kappa 0.85/0.80).
findings.support: S1 limitations section; S2; S13 Section 4.1

findings.claim: In patient-safety incident reporting, ML studies tend to replace the reporters' categories with expert labels rather than use them (three experts, kappa 0.93). No study found measures how often reporters pick the wrong event type.
findings.support: S23 Methods

findings.claim: Aviation: ASRS primary-problem codes are assigned by NASA analysts, and SDR JASC codes are picked by the filer from a drop-down. NHTSA recall component codes are assigned by NHTSA with acknowledged subjectivity; owner complaints let the filer pick up to three components (search snippet only). No measured agreement between filed codes and an expert re-read was found for SDR, ASRS or NHTSA.
findings.support: S14 Sections 3-4; S15

findings.claim: In label-noise research, a per-filer house style counts as annotator-dependent and instance-dependent noise. The standard tools: per-annotator confusion matrices learned with the classifier (works with one label per item), Dawid-Skene-style estimation (an EM method that infers true labels from several noisy labellers), and annotator-disjoint test splits. Instance-dependent noise is acknowledged as under-studied.
findings.support: S18; S19 abstract; S20 abstract; S21 Section II

findings.claim: Accepted minimum designs for a validated subset: a random or stratified sample of 50-500 items; two independent readers with a third to settle disagreements, or 3-5 experts for a test set; agreement reported as Cohen kappa or Krippendorff alpha, with about 0.8 as the usual bar. Precedents: Lalani (two authors, up to 50 reports per term plus a random 1,000), Edin 2026 (50 random cases per code), CWE audit (two authors, kappa 0.87, 100-item benchmark), CheXpert (200 items by 3 readers, 500 by 5).
findings.support: S8; S4; S10; S16; S22 Section 4.1

findings.claim: On noisy test sets, ranking models against the noisy key can flip once the key is corrected: smaller models can overtake larger ones after correction.
findings.support: S17 abstract

gaps: No published study audits MAUDE device-problem codes (IMDRF Annex A) against an expert re-read. The FDA page says submitters enter them and does not say they are validated.
No reporter-versus-expert misclassification rate was found for hospital patient-safety event types; only reviewer-versus-reviewer kappas (0.73, 0.93) and descriptions of the problem.
No agreement study was found for FAA SDR JASC codes, ASRS analyst codes or NHTSA complaint components. A 1991 GAO review of SDR data quality was seen only as a search snippet.
Who assigns MedDRA terms in FAERS (manufacturer vs FDA) could not be confirmed from FDA pages.
Edin et al. 2026 is a preprint and contradicts itself (66-72% in the abstract, 76-86% in the conclusion). The number of reviewers in its manual review is not stated in the part read.
The Nong et al. 2026 CWE audit uses an LLM-based audit tool. Its 3.63% error rate rests on that tool plus human confirmation of flagged cases, not on a fully human-read random sample.

Not opened: the Kralova 2023 COVID vaccine MedDRA audit and Toneatti 2006 (both known only via S7); Knisely et al. 2020 and Mishali et al. 2025 (MAUDE coding variation, cited by S11); the Fong et al. 2021 study on reclassifying 'miscellaneous' patient-safety reports.
No source gives a formal sample-size rule for validating a 471-class hierarchical code. The sample-size figures under implications are ordinary binomial arithmetic, not taken from a source.
The earlier-round numbers about the MAUDE key (wf1 files) were not re-checked; this pass did not depend on them.
implications: To the owner's first question: yes, the filed code is a noisy key, and every neighbouring field says so. The precedents show the noise is systematic per filer (house style, generic parent over specific child, habitual template codes). This matches what the project already sees in MAUDE: template texts with habitual codes, sibling and more-specific moves between years, and LLMs reading the text literally.

The project's gap between the encoder and the LLMs looks like the radiology ICD-10 case (S6): the fine-tuned encoder learns the filers' habit and wins against the filed code, while a literal reader loses against it. Whether the LLM is 'right' can only be settled against a human-validated subset, not against the filed code. The current three Opus readers do not count as such a subset.

The fairest framing is to report two tasks separately: (a) predict the code the filer would file (coding assistance, where the filed code is the right key) and (b) describe what the narrative says (needs an expert-validated key). ICD and CWE papers make this split implicitly.

Adopt the CWE three-way verdict for any human read: exact / defensible alternative (sibling, parent or child in Annex A) / contradicted by the text. Report the share in each, by stratum (rare vs frequent code, template vs unique narrative) and by manufacturer.

A minimal subset reviewers would likely accept: about 200 reports, sampled by stratum (for example, half from cases where the coders disagree with the filed code, half random, with rare codes over-sampled and reweighted back). Two independent human readers, ideally one with device or clinical engineering background, label blind to the source; a third settles disagreements. Report Cohen kappa or Krippendorff alpha on the three-way verdict and on the exact path.

Rough reading cost: Lalani and the CWE audit used author-readers on samples of 50 to a few hundred. With n=200 a proportion near 50% carries roughly plus or minus 7 points (95%); with n=100, about plus or minus 10.

Model the filer: the manufacturer is on every MAUDE report, like the CNA in CWE. Report accuracy per manufacturer, and test on manufacturers held out of training, as Geva et al. recommend for annotators. This would show directly how much of the encoder's lead is learned house style.

Do not copy the Muaz et al. LLM-agreement filter as the evaluation set: it keeps only reports where an LLM already agrees and so builds the bias into the benchmark. It can be cited as the only prior MAUDE coding benchmark, and as evidence that the community has not yet validated MAUDE codes.

To the owner's second question: MAUDE device-problem coding is barely used as a machine-learning benchmark (one LLM-filtered benchmark found, S11). A careful note on how good the key is would itself be a contribution, much as Searle 2020 and the 2026 CWE audit were for their fields.

checks.claim: Clinical ICD coding re-reads disagree a lot: UK median accuracy 83.2% (IQR 67.3-92.1, range 50.5-97.8); hired coders vs MIMIC micro-Jaccard 10.7; MDACE agreed on 45.1% of MIMIC inpatient codes; two coders alpha 0.53 -> 0.97 after review
checks.detail: All numbers are in the sources. Burns 2012 abstract (opened via Europe PMC, DOI 10.1093/pubmed/fdr054): 83.2%, IQR 67.3-92.1%, 50.5-97.8%, primary diagnoses 73.8% -> 96.0%. Kim and Ganapathi (arxiv.org/pdf/2107.10650, full text read): Table 1, human coders micro-Jaccard 10.7, precision 47.7, recall 12.1, RAC 42.0. But the two CPC coders picked codes from a shortlist of 4,075 in a web tool, about 30 hours over a week, and footnote 2 says neither code set is absolute truth. MDACE (aclanthology 2023.acl-long.416, full text read): Table 5 shows 2,370 of 5,250 (45.1%) agreed. The paper explains this partly by missing operative notes (over 37% of encounters; 33% of the missing inpatient codes) and by changed guidelines. Table 2 alpha 0.53/0.24 -> 0.97/0.96 came from two coders on three charts, and it measures agreement on evidence-span annotations, not only on code lists. The report presents it as code agreement.

checks.claim: Errors in filed codes are systematic; symptom codes over-used; 67% of replacements cross chapter/category; MAP 88.5% vs original, 48.1% vs validated
checks.detail: Kim, Li, Ye, Tahmasebi, Aslam, arXiv 2103.07808 (full text read). 29,826 radiology notes were each reviewed by at least two expert coders, with a more experienced third coder settling disagreements. Original-vs-validator agreement was 65% and validator-vs-validator 72%, and validators could see the original codes. The 67% applies only to the 'replacement' disagreement type, which covers 14.0% of notes (Table 1-2), not to all disagreements. Section 3.1: MAP on the top-100 codes was 88.5% against original labels and 48.1% against validated labels, computed for one site (1,688 notes). The authors call the noise systematic and describe symptom codes being over-predicted.

checks.claim: Danish coding: model right in 66-72% of disagreements (abstract) or 76-86% (conclusion); 50-case reviews found 74-76%; cause linked to reimbursement
checks.detail: Edin et al., arXiv 2603.00221v2 (full text read). The report has the locations reversed. The abstract says 76-86%; the 66-72% figure is in the introduction's contribution list. The paper is internally inconsistent, but the report puts the inconsistency in the wrong sections. Section 2.4: 50 randomly sampled model-identified uncoded cases per condition: suicide-related 86%, weight disorders 76% explicit, hypertension 74% explicit (plus 10% on medication only). The review covers only cases the model added that humans had not coded, not disagreements in general. The paper does not say who did the review or that the reviewers were experts. The original codes came from physicians and medical secretaries, not professional coders. The reimbursement link is confirmed (Section 3).

checks.claim: CWE three-way verdict: 49.7% exact, 31.4% defensible, 3.6% wrong; ~70-point exact-match spread by CNA; true errors vary less
checks.detail: Nong, Du, Behravan, Cai, arXiv 2608.21977 (abstract page and full PDF read). Table 4: S1 49.70%, S2 overlap 25.01% + S3 defensible 6.36% (= 31.37%), S4 inconsistent 3.63% (564 CVEs). There is also a 15.30% category where the classifier was wrong and the NVD label was right. All shares are measured against an LLM-agent (CWEAgent/Arbitrator) label, not a human read. Of the 564 flagged labels, two authors confirmed 434 (kappa 0.87), so confirmed errors are about 2.8%, not 3.6% 'clearly wrong'. The text says 'roughly 70-point' exact-match range across CNAs, and the S4 spread is narrower (confirmed). The top-15 rows of Table 10 show only about 39-84%.

checks.claim: MedDRA: Norwegian coders 36% exact match; 65.8% of substitutions within same HLT; VAERS 93.4% correct with kappa 0.55
checks.detail: Garmann T, Samdal H, Sartori D, Jahanlu D, Andersen F, Rocca E, Drug Saf 2025;48(11):1253-1269 (PMC12515201, read): 26 coders, 11 deliberately ambiguous tasks, 286 answers, 103 (36%) matched; 65.8/23.7/10.5%. Kim and Nakashole, Findings EMNLP 2023 (PDF read, Section 4.1): VAERS uses certified MedDRA coders, 93.4% of 1,000 symptoms judged correct, Fleiss kappa 0.55. The raters were Amazon Mechanical Turk crowd workers, not experts. The 36% comes from tasks chosen to be hard, so it is not a population error rate.

checks.claim: MAUDE event type: 23% of reports describing a death filed as other categories; manufacturers choose >95%; no published audit of MAUDE device-problem codes
checks.detail: Lalani et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021, doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.3942 (PMC8314174, read). 23% (95% CI 20-25%) and missed deaths 17% (16-19%) are confirmed. 7,951 reports were reviewed by hand plus a random 1,000. Manufacturers filed 95.9% (278,251 of 290,141) and choose the category on more than 95% of reports. The answer text wrongly cites this as [S12] (the FDA page) instead of S8. I also found no hand audit of device-problem codes. The closest are Choi et al. 2024 (regulators coding six vignettes diverged) and the BMJ 2026 summary-report audit (see missed).

checks.claim: Only MAUDE coding benchmark keeps records where one LLM agrees with the filed code at Level 2; 10,000 -> 2,899 -> 1,728; no human validation
checks.detail: eprints.dkit.ie/1049 PDF (full text extracted). Authors: Muhammad Muaz, Zaar Haider Janjua, Roisin Loughran, Niamh St John Lynch (the report's author order differs). Filter: Gemini Flash 3, Level 2 reconciliation. 10000 -> 2899 after cleaning -> 1728 device-problem records (40% reduction). GPT-OSS-120B reached 59.49% at Level 1 and 23.04% at Level 3. No human validation; the authors themselves say future work should replicate the step with multiple LLMs. The abstract says 'LLMs' in the plural, but the body names one model. The authors attribute most discards to strategically hedged narratives and 'a smaller fraction' to genuine coding errors, citing Mishali 2025. They also say regulatory-affairs or QA staff at manufacturers do the coding.

checks.claim: ICD ML practice: filed code accepted as gold, errors listed as limitation; some add expert subsets (MDACE) or a silver standard (Searle, kappa 0.85/0.80)
checks.detail: Edin et al. SIGIR 2023 (arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10909, text extracted): the limitations section says manual coding is error-prone and partly subjective, cites 83.2% and Searle's 35%, and suggests human-in-the-loop evaluation (confirmed). Searle 2020 (aclanthology 2020.bionlp-1.8, abstract read): its own abstract says the most frequent codes are 'undercoded up to 35%', so the report's claim that S1 'overstates' Searle is weak. I did not re-check the kappas. 'Common practice' rests on one paper.

checks.claim: Patient-safety incident ML replaces reporter categories with expert labels (three experts, kappa 0.93); no reporter-vs-expert rate found
checks.detail: Wang et al. BMC Med Inform Decis Mak 2017 (PMC5468980, read): three experts validated labels, kappa 0.93, and reporters 'may not be expert in incident classification'. Luschi et al. Heliyon 2023 (PMC10638042, read) likewise used expert-labelled MAUDE reports rather than MAUDE codes, with no stated agreement.

checks.claim: ASRS codes by NASA analysts; SDR JASC picked by filer from drop-down; NHTSA codes; no agreement studies
checks.detail: FAA SDRS Field Instructions (PDF text extracted): JASC/ATA chosen from a drop-down table, and 'select one to three' nature-of-condition codes (confirmed). Ihshaish et al. arXiv 2609.16267 exists (abstract read: ASRS and NHTSA, with a recommendation to report how record and label were produced). I did not verify the ASRS/NHTSA detail claims in its body.

checks.claim: Label-noise tools: per-annotator confusion matrices, Dawid-Skene, annotator-disjoint splits; instance-dependent noise under-studied
checks.detail: Geva et al. arXiv 1908.07898 (abstract read): annotator IDs help, models generalise poorly to unseen annotators, test annotators should be disjoint. Here the annotators wrote the examples, which matches MAUDE manufacturers who write both text and code. I did not re-open Raykar, Tanno or Song; the report itself saw only abstracts for the first two.

checks.claim: Minimum validated-subset designs (50-500 items, 2 readers + adjudicator, kappa/alpha ~0.8)
checks.detail: The precedents check out: Lalani (manual review of 7,951 plus a random 1,000, not 'up to 50 per term'; they reviewed all reports for 44 terms and random samples for 18), Edin 2026 (50 per condition, reviewer count unstated), CWE (two authors, kappa 0.87, 100-CVE benchmark), Kim 2021 (2 coders + third). No source sets a minimum design. The report's 'about 200' is its own suggestion.

checks.claim: Model rankings can flip after test-label correction
checks.detail: Northcutt et al. 2021 (arXiv 2103.14749) was not re-opened in this pass. The report saw the abstract only. The claim matches the well-known abstract but is unverified here.

bad_sources: Answer text cites [S12] (FDA MAUDE page) for the 23% death-misclassification figure; that figure is from S8 (Lalani et al. 2021).

S4 (Edin et al. 2026): report says the abstract gives 66-72% and the conclusion 76-86%; actually the abstract gives 76-86% and the 66-72% is in the introduction. Reviewers are not stated to be experts.
S11 author order is wrong: the PDF lists Muhammad Muaz, Zaar Haider Janjua, Roisin Loughran, Niamh St John Lynch.
S10: '3.6% clearly wrong' misstates 'likely errors' flagged by an LLM agent; only 434/15,556 (~2.8%) were human-confirmed.
corrections: The 23% of death reports filed as non-death is Lalani et al. 2021 (S8), not the FDA page.

Edin 2026: abstract = 76-86%, introduction = 66-72%. The figures cover model-added codes that humans omitted (secondary diagnoses), reviewed on 50 random cases per condition by unstated reviewers. The Danish codes came from physicians and secretaries, not professional coders.
CWE audit: all shares are relative to an LLM-agent label. Human-confirmed mislabels are 434 of 15,556 (~2.8%). A further 15.3% of disagreements were the tool's error with the NVD label correct.

MDACE: the 0.53 -> 0.97 alpha is agreement on evidence spans for three charts. The 45.1% overlap is partly explained by missing operative notes (33% of missing inpatient codes) and changed guidelines.

Kim and Ganapathi 2021: the 10.7 micro-Jaccard comes from coders working in a shortlist web tool for about 30 hours; the authors say neither set is ground truth. It should not be read as a measured error rate of MIMIC codes.
Kim et al. 2021 radiology: validators saw the original codes; the 67% figure applies to replacement-type disagreements only (14% of notes).
VAERS 93.4% was judged by MTurk crowd workers (2-of-3 majority), not experts.
'Most ML papers treat filed code as gold' rests on one paper (S1); state it as an observation, not a measured share.

On 'does everyone use this data': MAUDE itself is widely used in device-safety research (Li et al. 2024 found 60 MAUDE studies with executable queries and low reproducibility). What is rare is using its device-problem codes as an ML answer key.
missed: Choi SJ et al. 'The application study of harmonization code in medical device adverse event reporting', BMC Health Serv Res 2024, doi:10.1186/s12913-024-11885-1 (abstract only, via Europe PMC REST search). 29 regulators coded six virtual adverse-event vignettes with IMDRF codes. Most chose broad level-1 codes over level 2/3, choices were diverse, and over 50% picked the intended codes only in case 6. This is the closest direct evidence on IMDRF code consistency, and the report missed it.

BMJ 2026 cross-sectional study of MAUDE summary reports, doi:10.1136/bmj-2026-100812 (read only BMJ press page https://bmjgroup.com/medical-device-adverse-event-reports-are-often-incomplete-inaccurate-and-delayed/): of 6,308 summary reports (Jul 2019-Jun 2025), 57% identified no device or use problem, 38% reported insufficient information and 11% were wrongly flagged as non-summary. This is a recent audit of MAUDE coding fields.

Schroll JB, Maund E, Gotzsche PC. Challenges in Coding Adverse Events in Clinical Trials: A Systematic Review. PLoS One 2012;7(7):e41174 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3401103/, read). Only one study measured interobserver variation (12% different Preferred Terms), physicians judged about 8% of codes to deviate from the descriptions, and the review found little evidence that AE coding is reliable or reproducible.

Mishali M, Sheffer N, Mishali O, Negev M. Understanding Variation Among Medical Device Reporting Sources: A Study of the MAUDE Database. Clin Ther 2025;47(1):76-81, doi:10.1016/j.clinthera.2024.10.004 (search snippet only). Code use varies strongly by reporter type. Muaz et al. cite it for genuine human coding errors.

Li X, Feng Y, Gong Y, Chen Y. Assessing the Reproducibility of Research Based on the FDA MAUDE Data. J Patient Saf 2024;20(5):e45-e58 (search snippet only; reference also seen in Muaz PDF). 60 MAUDE studies with executable queries had low reproducibility. This shows MAUDE is widely used for surveillance research, not as an ML benchmark.

Shi Y, Gong Y. Leveraging LLMs to Understand Narratives in MAUDE Reports. Stud Health Technol Inform vol 323 (https://ebooks.iospress.nl/doi/10.3233/SHTI250076, abstract read). GPT-4-turbo finds uncoded surgical procedures in endoscopic-clip narratives; it does not classify device-problem codes.

Luschi A, Nesi P, Iadanza E. Heliyon 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10638042/, read). ClinicalBERT on 3,075 MAUDE reports with expert HIT/non-HIT labels instead of MAUDE codes; the authors found some expert labels wrong too. Another sign that MAUDE ML work avoids the filed codes.
check.net: Partly, yes. In every neighbouring field where the person or organisation that files a record also picks its code, careful re-readers often disagree with that code, and much of the disagreement is systematic. ICD radiology shows 65% exact agreement with expert validators, and a model scored 88.5% MAP against the filed codes but 48.1% against the validated ones. In UK routine data the median accuracy is 83.2%. MedDRA coders agree poorly on ambiguous terms, and in NVD CWE labels the filing organisation drives precision more than outright error (human-confirmed errors about 2.8%; most disagreement is imprecision). For MAUDE itself, the filer-chosen event type misfiles 23% of reports that describe a death (Lalani 2021). Regulators coding six vignettes with IMDRF codes chose diverse, mostly level-1 codes (Choi 2024). A 2026 BMJ audit found most MAUDE summary reports code 'no device problem' or 'insufficient information'. Nobody has published an expert re-read of MAUDE device-problem codes, so how wrong they are is unmeasured; 'wrong' also partly means 'a different but defensible level or sibling', not error. On the second question: MAUDE is heavily used for device-safety surveillance research (dozens of query-based studies), but almost no machine-learning work uses its device-problem codes as an answer key. The one benchmark (Muaz et al., AIAI 2026) keeps only reports where Gemini agrees with the filed code at Level 2, and other MAUDE NLP studies use expert labels instead of the filed codes.

lit.title: The same two questions for the second corpus, FAA Service Difficulty Reports

report.answer: The project's SDR label is PartCondition, a one-word condition term such as CORRODED, CRACKED or INOPERATIVE (scripts/sdr_data.py). It is not the JASC code. The person who files the report assigns it: the air carrier, operator or repair station mechanic. In the web form they pick it from a lookup list. Bulk filers using the batch format type it into a 16-character field, and the batch spec points to only a "recommended, standardized" list. For JASC the same spec says "must be a valid 4-digit code". The regulation (121.703(e)) asks for the nature of the failure and its apparent cause. It does not name a part-condition field. The FAA's own documents admit data-quality problems (GAO 1991; the 2000 rule change; InFO 16009 in 2016). GAO in 2010 rated SDRS as having no data-entry accuracy controls. Nobody has published how reliable PartCondition coding is. In the project's own SDR pool (214,601 reports, 2023 to Oct 2026), only 0.89% of reports have a narrative that was filed under more than one term, against 35.2% for MAUDE. Copying the label of an earlier identical narrative covers only 5.3% of 2026 reports, against 64.8% for MAUDE. Where the text says "crack", 92-99% of reports are labelled CRACKED at every large operator. Where the text says "INOP", the label depends on the airline: INOPERATIVE on 94.7% of Southwest's reports, but only 49.0% of United's and 60.8% of Delta's. So SDR is less of a filer's template habit than MAUDE, but more of a filer's vocabulary habit: the errors are about which synonym was used, not what went wrong. SDR is not a common ML dataset. It is used by FAA inspectors and reliability analysts, and a handful of papers use it: forecasting in the 1990s-2000, one binary depressurization classifier (2023) and one JASC-classification paper (2025). There is no shared benchmark for it. As far as I found, nobody has published PartCondition classification before this project.

sources.says: Each Part 121 certificate holder reports the listed failures (para a) plus any other failure it believes endangers safe operation. Reports cover 24-hour periods and are due within 96 hours, on a form or in a format acceptable to the Administrator. Required content (e) includes the nature of the failure, the part and system, the apparent cause (e.g. wear, crack, design deficiency, personnel error) and the action taken. There is no part-condition field and no JASC/ATA code requirement in the current text.

gaps: The text of 14 CFR 135.415 and 145.221 was not opened. Only the SDRS home page listing them as reporting rules was seen.
AC 20-109B (the current SDRS advisory circular) returned 403 to both fetch methods, so its PartCondition guidance and any data-use caveats are unverified.

The 'JASC Code, Standard Part Name and Condition' document and the SDRS Look-Up Tables zip were not opened. It is unknown how many standard condition terms exist and whether the web lookup forces a choice from them, so it is also unknown whether terms such as FAULTY or UNSERVICEABLE are on the list.
No study measures the accuracy or inter-coder agreement of PartCondition or JASC. The Verhagen & Scott 2025 full text (which might discuss mislabels) was not accessible; only the abstract was seen.
GAO RCED-91-24 was seen only as a summary; its detailed numbers were not read.
Niraula et al. 2023 and 2020 and Tanguy et al. 2016 were seen only through snippets; whether Niraula 2020 used SDR data is unverified.
The MaintNet aviation dataset size (6,169 entries) comes from a search summary, not an opened source.
The FAA/George Mason JASC-classification project (DOT-1000022) was noted in the earlier corpus search; no publication was found and it was not re-checked here.

The data look is light. Same-text conflict is a weak test because SDR narratives are mostly unique. The operator synonym tables show habit, but no human has read reports to judge whether, say, FAULTED vs INOPERATIVE carries a real difference. Whether the batch filers (large airlines) map internal codes automatically is unknown; this would explain the per-operator patterns but is not documented in anything read.
implications: For the owner's question: the SDR key is not 'wrong' in the MAUDE sense. Narratives are written per event and seldom copied (5% copy coverage vs 65%), and visible-damage terms such as CRACKED match the text more than 92% of the time. Its weakness is different: a flat list with near-synonyms, filled in by the filer with little checking, where the choice between FAILED, FAULTED, FAULTY, INOPERATIVE and MALFUNCTIONED largely tracks which airline filed.

Part of the error in the SDR results, which sit flat around 0.45-0.50 macro-F1 for the LLMs, is probably synonym or operator vocabulary rather than misreading. A cheap check is to re-score SDR with a pre-declared synonym merge (FAILED/FAULTED/FAULTY/INOPERATIVE/MALFUNCTIONED/DEFECTIVE/UNSERVICEABLE; LOW PRESSURE/PRESSURE LOSS; EXCESS PLAY/WORN) and to report accuracy by operator. If scores jump, the ceiling is the key, not the coders.

The project's exact-duplicate dedup keeps only the earliest report per narrative, so the 427 conflicting narratives are silently resolved to their first label. This affects under 1% of reports, so it is minor for SDR, unlike MAUDE.

Do not present SDR as a 'standard benchmark': it is a regulator's raw database that a handful of papers have used, with no shared split or label audit. Present it as a second real-world coded corpus and cite the FAA's own data-quality statements (InFO 16009; GAO-10-414 Figure 3) as known limits.

Comparison with MAUDE: the MAUDE device-problem code is more of a filer's habit at the template level, since one manufacturer template carries one habitual code and literal readings disagree with it. The SDR PartCondition is more of a filer's habit at the vocabulary level, since the same plain observation gets a different near-synonym depending on the airline. A model can learn MAUDE's habit by copying text, and SDR's habit only from the operator identity, which the project's coders do not see.

report.headline: The filed code depends mostly on the text the report contains, but that text is largely the filer's own template, so the two cannot be cleanly separated. For texts of equal similarity, the filer adds only a few points. Within one product code, two near-identical narratives (cosine 0.9 or higher) carry the same leaf code 91-93% of the time when two different companies filed them, and 93-94% when the same manufacturer filed both. Over product codes, a pair filed by the same manufacturer agrees on the leaf 2-5 points more often than a pair filed by different manufacturers at the same similarity (about 9 points at cosine 0.3-0.6). The bigger fact is that different companies rarely write similar text. At cosine 0.9 or higher there were 28,256 same-manufacturer pairs against only 1,374 cross-company pairs, and 72% of those cross-company pairs are dental implants. Knowing only the filer (manufacturer x product code majority) gets 0.485 of 2024val reports right. Adding a 60-character template gets 0.589 (0.716 weighted by n_reports), against 0.872 for the encoder and 0.344 / 0.377 for Qwen / Gemma zero-shot. 64.5% of what the encoder gets right is also right from filer plus template alone. Where the house style shows is in how specific a code a filer picks. For example, Tandem files 82% of 'Incorrect Measurement', while Dexcom and Abbott file the same kind of glucose-inaccuracy report under the parent code. Of the template groups where an LLM consistently differs from the filer, roughly 40% are parent/child or sibling pairs and roughly a third are different families. So an LLM answer that differs from the filed code is often a different but defensible place in the tree, not necessarily a wrong reading of the event. The pool the project uses covers only 37-52% of reports with a narrative; the rest is left out because of vague codes, multiple codes, or narratives filed under more than one code.

Within one product code (86 product codes with at least 2 manufacturers of at least 200 rows each; up to 5 manufacturers each), the code distributions of two manufacturers differ a lot: median Jensen-Shannon distance 0.767 (IQR 0.563-0.898, 309 pairs). findings.claim: Text and filer are entangled: similar text almost always comes from the same filer. Pair counts in the sample at cosine 0.9 or higher: 28,256 same-manufacturer, 3,932 different manufacturer name with the same first word (often the same company group), and 1,374 different company. 72% of those 1,374 cross-company pairs are dental implants (DZE). The pooled cross-company numbers are dominated by DZE in every similarity bin (72-93%).

Agreement ceiling for near-identical text (step 6): pairs at cosine 0.9 or higher from different companies in the same product code carry the same leaf code 0.921 of the time pooled (1,374 pairs) or 0.929 macro (7 product codes); level 1 is 0.94-0.99. Same-manufacturer near-identical pairs agree 0.941 (pooled). So even a perfect text reader cannot reach much above about 0.92-0.94 against this key on template-like reports. findings.evidence: s3b_results.json pairs_pooled and pairs_macro_prodcode for the 0.9 bin. Over all reports, 54.7% sit in codes where one manufacturer files at least half, and 20.2% in codes where one files at least 80%. Manufacturer name variants were not merged (e.g. ABBOTT VASCULAR vs ABBOTT VASCULAR INC.), so these shares are lower bounds.

The 46 rare codes have a median of 5 pool rows, a median top-manufacturer share of 0.5, a share of at least 0.5 for 67% of them, and a single manufacturer for 5 of them. The filer's habit lies mostly in how specific a code it picks (parent vs child, generic level-1 vs leaf) for its own templates, rather than in describing different events. Find why the 2025/2026 pools are smaller than 'single informative code minus conflict narratives' (about 382k and 256k reports).

Template = first 60 characters of the digit-masked, lowercased narrative. This is coarse and some different narratives share it.

Pair sampling: up to 800 rows per manufacturer and up to 5 manufacturers per product code. Pooled pair numbers are dominated by dental implants (DZE), so the macro averages over product codes are the ones to quote. The per-bin product-code sets differ and are small (7-62).
'Different company' = the first word of the manufacturer name differs. 'Different manufacturer string, same first word' is often the same company group.
The step 3 frequency bands use 2024 pool rows, not training counts. Rare-code concentration is based on about 5 reports each.
False-LLM-code counts are unweighted rows of the 2025/2026 natural samples summed over three LLMs. They are not natural-proportion estimates.

Step 5 reuses wf2/rawstream caches (copied), which use the first D narrative per report from the foitext zips. The vague set = the project's NON_INFORMATIVE codes plus A24-A27 from the code table, excluding 4077 (A2501), which the project treats as a label code.
The cosine 0.9 'ceiling' covers only template-like texts and only within a product code.
surprises: Even the same manufacturer, writing near-identical text (cosine 0.9 or higher), files a different leaf code about 6% of the time (pooled leaf agreement 0.941).

The pooled cross-company pairs show level-2 agreement of 0.96 at cosine 0.6-0.7, against 0.74 for same-manufacturer pairs. This is entirely a dental-implant (osseointegration) artifact, which is why the pooled table is misleading.

Medical-device house styles differ mostly in specificity: e.g. Tandem files 'Charging Problem' (parent) where the LLMs say 'Failure to Charge', and Dexcom and Abbott file the parent result-inaccuracy code where the LLMs pick a child.
The largest LLM-filer mismatch group in 2024val is a single recall template (Respironics sound-abatement foam, 508 rows / 1,084 reports) filed as 'Degraded'.

checks.claim: Filer-only baselines on 2024val: mfr x product 0.485/0.508, plus 60-char template 0.589/0.716; encoder 0.872/0.918, Qwen zs 0.344/0.359, Gemma zs 0.377/0.408, RAG 0.847/0.846; 4,625 and 5,629 of the encoder's 8,723 right answers also right by the filer rules; 227/257 filer-right-encoder-wrong; Qwen 1,940 of 3,443, Gemma 2,135 of 3,768
checks.detail: Measured with my own code (c1.py): every number reproduced exactly. A random 80/20 split with a different seed (7) gives 0.394/0.481 (mfr), 0.455/0.526 (mfr x prod), 0.560/0.679 (+template), close to theirs. Not leakage: pool rows are distinct masked narratives, and template overlap is what the rule is meant to use. Two additions. (1) The 60-char template alone, with no filer (backing off to product code only), already gets 0.531/0.661. So the filer adds about 6 points on top of the template, which supports 'mostly text'. (2) Where the filer+template rule is wrong, the encoder is still right 0.752 of the time (0.956 where the rule is right). So '64.5% of what the encoder gets right' does not mean the encoder only learned the filer. Merging manufacturer-name variants (suffix normalisation, 2,428 to 1,957 names) changes the mfr x product score by less than 0.001.

checks.claim: House style at equal similarity is small: same-manufacturer vs different-manufacturer leaf agreement (macro over product codes) 0.472 vs 0.384 at cos 0.3-0.6 ... 0.933 vs 0.911 at 0.9+
checks.detail: Measured: in my own pair sample (different seed, IDF fitted within each product code, 7.1M pairs at cos>=0.3), same-string vs different-string macro leaf agreement is 0.547/0.497 (57 product codes), 0.734/0.697, 0.811/0.800, 0.907/0.885, 0.942/0.913 (14). The per-product median gap is about 0 from 0.6 to 0.9 (-0.003, -0.019, -0.008) and +0.025 at 0.9+. So 'small' holds. But what is compared is mostly not two companies (see next check). Under my corporate-group merge, a same-group vs different-group macro can be formed only for 2 product codes at 0.6-0.8 (FMI, GEX) and for none at 0.9+. The 'house style at equal text' question across independent companies cannot be answered from this sample.

checks.claim: Near-identical narratives (cos>=0.9) from two different companies carry the same leaf 91-93% of the time; 1,374 cross-company pairs, 72% dental implants (DZE)
checks.detail: Measured (c3.py): the 'different company' label (first word of the name differs) is almost all one corporate group. Of my 1,078 such pairs at cos>=0.9, 71.7% are DZE (their 72% reproduced). The top pairs are Straumann-Anthogyr (337), JJGC-Anthogyr (241), Straumann-JJGC (195), Concord Manufacturing-Erika de Reynosa (173; FKX dialysis), Medtronic Puerto Rico-Medtronic Chengdu (38), Covidien-US Surgical Puerto Rico (20), St. Jude Neuromodulation-Abbott Medical (20) and Embecta-BD Dun Laoghaire (17). With a hand-made corporate-group map, 98.1% of these pairs are same-group. The map is inferred from general knowledge of ownership (JJGC = Neodent and Anthogyr both Straumann Group; Erika de Reynosa and Concord = Fresenius; Covidien = Medtronic; St. Jude = Abbott) and was not checked against a source. After the merge, only 20 different-group pairs remain at cos>=0.9 (17 of them Embecta vs BD, a 2022 spin-off from one plant; leaf agreement 0.95). At cos 0.6-0.9 there are 507 such pairs, against about 720k same-group pairs. So the cross-company number of about 0.92 is really the agreement between plants or brands of one corporate group.

checks.claim: Agreement ceiling: even a perfect text reader cannot reach much above about 0.92-0.94 against this key on template-like reports
checks.detail: Pair agreement is not an accuracy ceiling. For a text cluster with code shares p, pair agreement is sum p^2 but the best reader gets max p, which is at least as high. Measured: for pool rows with at least one cos>=0.9 neighbour in my sample (16,333 rows), copying the majority code of the neighbours is right 0.922 of rows but 0.982 of reports weighted by n_reports (0.989 at cos>=0.95). In raw 2024 single-informative-code reports before the pool drops conflicts, reports sharing an identical masked narrative agree 0.966 pairwise (pooled), 0.945 averaged over narratives, and the majority code covers 0.973 of those 1,446,573 reports. Only 6,689 of 90,187 multi-report narratives are conflicts. So on template text the key is about 97-98% self-consistent by reports. The 0.92-0.94 figure is a row-level pair statistic and understates the ceiling.

checks.claim: Tandem files 82% of 'Incorrect Measurement' while Dexcom and Abbott file the same kind of glucose-inaccuracy report under the parent code (house style lies in specificity)
checks.detail: Measured: the 82% is right (7,622 reports, Tandem 0.820). But 4 of 4 randomly sampled Tandem 'Incorrect Measurement' rows are pump insulin-gauge (cartridge level) complaints ('the insulin gauge was inaccurate'), not glucose readings. Dexcom's parent-code rows are CGM vs BG-meter inaccuracy and Abbott's are erroneous glucose results. These are different events, not one event at two levels of specificity. The sample is small (4 per group), but the example cannot support the 'specificity' claim. Also, Abbott Diabetes Care files the parent on 46.1% of its reports but the children 'Low Readings' (14.5%) and 'High Readings' (14.2%) on 29%, so 'Abbott files the parent' is only partly true.

checks.claim: About 40% of consistent-mismatch groups are parent/child or sibling and about a third different family, so an LLM answer that differs from the filed code is often a defensible place in the tree
checks.detail: I did not recompute the group counts. Their log shows 16/41 (Qwen) and 13/38 (Gemma), which is 39% and 34%, so 'roughly 40%' fits Qwen only. But these groups hold only 976 of 6,557 (Qwen) and 969 of 6,232 (Gemma) disagreements. Measured over ALL 2024val zero-shot disagreements: different level-1 family 52.8% (Qwen), 48.3% (Gemma); parent/child 24.4%, 27.9%; sibling 10.0%, 9.5%; same family other branch 12.8%, 14.3%. On the 2026 natural samples: Opus 48.3% different family, 18.5% parent/child, 9.7% sibling; Qwen 45.3/19.0/11.1; Gemma 49.5/16.8/9.7. So about half of LLM disagreements are in a different top-level family, and only 28-38% are parent/child or sibling. The headline generalisation is overstated.

checks.claim: Pool covers 37-52% of reports with a narrative; the rest is left out because of vague codes, multiple codes or conflict narratives; 2025/2026 pools are about 382k/256k smaller for an unknown reason
checks.detail: Measured: the reason is documented in scripts/maude_pool.py (docstring lines 14-17, code lines 88-90). For 2025/2026 a narrative whose masked text is already in the 2024 pool is dropped. In raw 2025, 382,013 non-conflict single-code reports have text in the 2024 pool, leaving 1,058,842 against a pool sum of 1,059,165. The 323 difference is likely because the 2025 pool used the 2026-10-06 problem file and the raw scan the 2026-11-04 one (inferred). For 2026: 256,200 dropped, leaving 1,099,828, an exact match. So 'the rest' also includes texts already seen in the training year (13% of 2025 reports with a narrative, 10% of 2026). Coverage shares 52.3/36.7/41.4% reproduced from the same counts.

checks.claim: Codes the LLMs name falsely are in effect one filer's: Unintended Application Program Shut Down Dexcom 91.8%, Failure to Transmit Record iRhythm 69%, Wireless Communication Problem MiniMed 62%; Ventec 'Output Problem' 67%, Hamilton 'Defective Component' 20%
checks.detail: Measured: 0.918, 0.690, 0.616 by n_reports; Ventec in CBK 0.665, Hamilton 0.197 (by rows). Wireless Communication Problem is shared with Dexcom (33.6%), so 'one filer' is a stretch there. I did not recompute the false counts (408, 553 and so on).
